viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_en:
Remarks from Anthropic CEO @DarioAmodei on our initial public offering:

My co-founders and I started Anthropic because we believe that the most powerful technology of our time should be built for the benefit of humankind.

Daniela and I lost our father to a disease that, just a few years later, became curable. I started my career in biology, hoping to help future cures come sooner. In the lab, I saw the vast thicket of complexity that scientists face when they’re trying to understand disease and develop new treatments.

So many of the scientific tools that can cut through that thicket—tools for gene editing, gene synthesis, controlling brain cells with light—started as pure ideas. In other words, they came from thinking. From intelligence.

Human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world. But progress on other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families. Going from a great idea to a treatment can take decades: it took many years from the first discovery of a strange repeating pattern in DNA to the approval of the first treatment for a disease using CRISPR.

Nature is full of these patterns. But we’ve had too little intelligence to decipher most of them; too few scientists, with too little time. Now we can build that intelligence. Whether it’s protein folding, drug design, cancer genetics, or clinical trial administration, scientists across many areas of biology and medicine are finding Claude can help them do their research in a fraction of the time it would’ve taken just a couple of years ago. I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade.

I don’t want to get ahead of myself. At this point all we have are early results. Experiments and clinical trials will still take time. And although they involve slow and ponderous processes, I believe those processes can be substantially accelerated by AI. We hope that in the future fewer families miss a cure by just a few years.

Medicine is just a particularly vivid example, but there are many others. Our customers—the world’s most ambitious companies, nonprofits, and individual people—are already applying the intelligence we’ve built to stimulate economic growth; lift people out of poverty; protect democracy and free societies; even make everyday services like the DMV work better. We’re proud to work alongside them. And I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future.

At the same time, we have always been honest that this technology has very real risks. These range from misuse of the technology by individuals or nation-states, to economic disruption, to losing control of AI systems. We discuss these risks not because we think they are inevitable, but because we think they are avoidable.

Avoiding them depends on the choices made by the people building AI. There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety, versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety. And an obsession with safety and with public benefit has been woven into Anthropic’s DNA from the start. From safeguards against biological and cyber risks, to alignment training and testing, to looking inside our models like an X-ray, Anthropic has pioneered methods for understanding and steering the behavior of AI systems.

There is much work still to be done, and the most difficult safety work lies ahead of us. The incredible talent of the company that has enabled us to build the most capable AI systems will need to be directed, even more so than it has already, towards double- and triple-checking that those AI systems are safe and secure.

And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control. We will not bend to either business or political pressure. Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing.

If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top. When the race to the top is working properly, it doesn’t matter which company has the best models—everyone wins because everyone is building safely. The race to the top works best when driven from the front of the pack, and we fully hope and expect to do so, but the goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time.

The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history, and we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better.

This moment is bigger than any one company, or any one country. It will take all of us, working together, to ensure this technology goes well for us and the many generations to come. Starting today, we hope that you’ll join us on this mission.
viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_zh:
Anthropic 首席执行官 @DarioAmodei 关于我们首次公开募股的评论：

我和我的联合创始人创立了 Anthropic，因为我们相信我们这个时代最强大的技术应该是为了造福人类而构建的。

丹妮拉和我的父亲因一种疾病去世，仅仅几年后，这种疾病就可以治愈。我的职业生涯始于生物学，希望能帮助未来的治愈方法早日到来。在实验室里，我看到了科学家在试图了解疾病和开发新疗法时所面临的巨大复杂性。

许多能够突破这一困境的科学工具——基因编辑、基因合成、用光控制脑细胞的工具——都是从纯粹的想法开始的。换句话说，它们来自于思考。来自智力。

人类智慧已经让世界上大部分地区的鼠疫、天花和脊髓灰质炎等疾病成为历史。但对于如此多的患者及其家人来说，其他疾病的进展太慢了。从一个伟大的想法到一种治疗方法可能需要数十年的时间：从首次发现 DNA 中奇怪的重复模式到第一个使用 CRISPR 治疗疾病的方法获得批准，花了很多年的时间。

大自然充满了这些模式。但我们的智慧太少，无法破译其中的大部分。科学家太少，时间太少。现在我们可以构建这种智能。无论是蛋白质折叠、药物设计、癌症遗传学还是临床试验管理，生物学和医学许多领域的科学家都发现克劳德可以帮助他们完成研究，所需时间只是几年前的一小部分。我相信足够强大的人工智能，与人类协同工作，可以将一个世纪的科学和医学进步压缩为十年。

我不想超越自己。目前我们所拥有的只是早期结果。实验和临床试验仍需要时间。尽管它们涉及缓慢而繁重的过程，但我相信人工智能可以大大加速这些过程。我们希望未来能有更少的家庭因仅仅几年的时间而错过治疗。

医学只是一个特别生动的例子，但还有很多其他例子。我们的客户——世界上最雄心勃勃的公司、非营利组织和个人——已经在应用我们构建的智能来刺激经济增长；让人们摆脱贫困；保护民主和自由社会；甚至让 DMV 等日常服务更好地运作。我们很自豪能与他们一起工作。我对我们未来可以一起做的事情非常乐观。

与此同时，我们一直诚实地认为这项技术存在非常现实的风险。这些问题包括个人或民族国家滥用技术、经济混乱、失去对人工智能系统的控制等。我们讨论这些风险不是因为我们认为它们是不可避免的，而是因为我们认为它们是可以避免的。

避免它们取决于构建人工智能的人们做出的选择。如果我们不关心安全，人工智能将会如何发展，而如果我们痴迷于安全，人工智能将会如何发展，两者之间存在着巨大的差异。对安全和公共利益的痴迷从一开始就融入了 Anthropic 的基因中。从防范生物和网络风险，到校准训练和测试，再到像 X 射线一样观察我们的模型，Anthropic 开创了理解和引导人工智能系统行为的方法。

任重而道远，最艰巨的安全工作还在后面。该公司拥有令人难以置信的人才，使我们能够构建最强大的人工智能系统，我们需要对其进行双重和三重检查，以确保这些人工智能系统的安全性，甚至比现在更加努力。

明确地说，我们将加快人工智能系统的训练和部署步伐，只要有必要，我们就确信它们是安全的，并将继续处于人类控制之下。我们不会屈服于商业或政治压力。今天，公司的财务状况变得更加强大，这样做只会增强我们做正确事情的决心。

如果我们能够证明我们可以在安全方面做出正确的选择，同时仍能打造一家极其成功的公司，那么我们行业的其他人也会受到启发，采取同样的做法。我们称之为登顶竞赛。当竞争顺利进行时，哪家公司拥有最好的模型并不重要——每个人都会赢，因为每个人都在安全地建造。当处于领先地位时，通往顶峰的竞争效果最好，我们完全希望并期望这样做，但目标是让整个行业变得更好，无论 Anthropic 在任何特定时间是赢还是输。

机器智能的出现是人类历史上的开创性时刻之一，我们有一个难得的机会来让它变得更好。

这一刻比任何一家公司或任何一个国家都重要。我们所有人都需要共同努力，才能确保这项技术为我们和子孙后代带来良好的发展。从今天开始，我们希望您能加入我们的行列。

top_three.title: Apple is hiring engineers to build its own AI agent
top_three.title_en: Apple is hiring engineers to build its own AI agent
top_three.author: Emma Roth
top_three.article_content:
Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That’s according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which says Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant.

An AI agent from Apple would put the iPhonemaker in the running to compete with the likes of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Duet, and Google’s Tasks. Muse, ChatGPT, and Perplexity can already take control of a computer through their Mac apps, while Google just started letting Gemini do the same.

Apple began rolling out its AI-upgraded Siri in September, which you can use to ask questions about what’s on your screen, as well as perform actions across apps. It looks like Apple is planning to give Siri more agentic capabilities, as a report from Bloomberg suggests the company could add the ability to rotate and crop images in Photos, or organize Safari tabs. This lines up with the company’s new job listing, which says the engineer will work closely with teams across its Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models divisions.

“People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service,” the job listing says. “We’re building AI agents that can do the same… These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.”

With its upcoming iOS 27.3 update, Apple is also giving developers the ability to integrate Siri AI into “all apps.” This is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview and will eventually allow Siri to perform tasks across a wider range of apps.

This marks a paradigm shift in human-computer interaction, transforming AI models from mere assistants into autonomous system operators, which effectively challenges the traditional interface value of third-party applications.

Inception introduced Mercury 3 on October 19, 2026, describing the model as the most capable diffusion-based large language model released to date, with launch pricing of $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.35 per million output tokens.

The company said Mercury 3 outperforms GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 across a range of benchmarks while running four to eight times faster at more than 1,000 tokens per second. The announcement lists a speed of 1,068 tokens per second on NVIDIA GPUs and a context window of one million tokens, up from 260,000 tokens for Mercury 2.5. List pricing stands at $0.20 per million input tokens and $0.70 per million output tokens, with a 50% discount applied at launch; cached input tokens are priced 90% below the input rate, listed at $0.02 per million tokens and $0.01 under the promotion.

Inception framed the release as evidence that text diffusion scales. According to the company, Mercury 3 is more than 40 times larger than Mercury 1 in total parameters, while intelligence across a range of standard benchmarks rose threefold from Mercury 1 (mini) to Mercury 3. Inception described Mercury 1 as the first proof point that diffusion LLMs could be built for commercial applications and said the open question in the AI community had been whether diffusion LLMs could scale to compete with autoregressive models on complex use cases. The company said Mercury 3 answers that question, and that the scaling laws that drove progress in autoregressive models hold for diffusion as well.

Inception said early-access partners are already running Mercury 3 in latency-sensitive applications including browser-use agents, interactive education, real-time search agents, and customer support. Shuhao Zhang, cofounder of TinyFish AI, said in the announcement that his company ran Mercury 3 inside its production web-agent harness against frontier models on 50 live Mind2Web navigation tasks, where Mercury 3 completed 50% of them, which he described as significantly more than GPT-6.1-Sol, using the same token volume and the same number of agent steps at a fraction of the per-token cost.

Michael Tong, co-founder and CTO of General Learning, known as RevisionDojo, said Mercury 3 let the tutoring company give every student instant feedback “without giving up reasoning,” with hints, marked answers, and definitions returning in about a second at q...

top_three.title: Sources: National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is leaving now to let the White House get a successor confirmed before Democrats take the Senate in January (Axios)
top_three.title_en: Sources: National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is leaving now to let the White House get a successor confirmed before Democrats take the Senate in January (Axios)

inline_images.caption: White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross (left), who is leaving his post, with President Trump during an Oval Office event on June 22. Photo: Andrew
inline_images.alt: White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross (left), who is leaving his post, with President

top_three.author: Axios
top_three.article_content:
White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross is leaving his post, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: Cairncross did not want to serve another two years and is leaving now to give the White House time to secure Senate confirmation before Democrats take control in January, two sources said.

The background: Cairncross leads the Office of the National Cyber Director, which coordinates cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government.

Case in point: He held technical meetings with Anthropic leaders over the summer after Commerce Department export controls effectively scrubbed the company's models from the internet.

Catch up quick: Cairncross brought experience in Republican politics and national security, having worked with the intelligence community and dealt with cyber threats at the Republican National Committee.

The big picture: The latest turnover in cyber personnel comes as the country grapples with critical infrastructure outages and increasingly powerful AI poised to empower cyber defenders and hackers alike.

What we're watching: Trump is also filling other key cyber positions.

Simultaneously, Arizona authorities initiated a landmark criminal investigation into OpenAI and peers over reports of rogue AI agents, bringing agentic OS control into direct collision with systemic legal liability.

news.title: Sources: Nvidia is in advanced talks to acquire diffusion LLM developer Inception for $500M+ plus earnouts; talks began before Jensen Huang's resignation (The Information)
news.title_en: Sources: Nvidia is in advanced talks to acquire diffusion LLM developer Inception for $500M+ plus earnouts; talks began before Jensen Huang's resignation (The Information)
news.author: The Information
news.article_content:
Key Points Mercury 3's launch pricing undercuts frontier rivals while claiming four to eight times…View moreMercury 3's launch pricing undercuts frontier rivals while claiming four to eight times their speed.Inception argues diffusion scaling laws now hold, with Mercury 3 over 40 times larger than Mercury 1.Early partners report Mercury 3 completing 50% of live Mind2Web navigation tasks against frontier models. Inception introduced Mercury 3 on October 19, 2026, describing the model as the most capable diffusion-based large language model released to date, with launch pricing of $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.35 per million output tokens.

The company said Mercury 3 outperforms GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 across a range of benchmarks while running four to eight times faster at more than 1,000 tokens per second. The announcement lists a speed of 1,068 tokens per second on NVIDIA GPUs and a context window of one million tokens, up from 260,000 tokens for Mercury 2.5. List pricing stands at $0.20 per million input tokens and $0.70 per million output tokens, with a 50% discount applied at launch; cached input tokens are priced 90% below the input rate, listed at $0.02 per million tokens and $0.01 under the promotion.

Inception framed the release as evidence that text diffusion scales. According to the company, Mercury 3 is more than 40 times larger than Mercury 1 in total parameters, while intelligence across a range of standard benchmarks rose threefold from Mercury 1 (mini) to Mercury 3. Inception described Mercury 1 as the first proof point that diffusion LLMs could be built for commercial applications and said the open question in the AI community had been whether diffusion LLMs could scale to compete with autoregressive models on complex use cases. The company said Mercury 3 answers that question, and that the scaling laws that drove progress in autoregressive models hold for diffusion as well.

Inception said early-access partners are already running Mercury 3 in latency-sensitive applications including browser-use agents, interactive education, real-time search agents, and customer support. Shuhao Zhang, cofounder of TinyFish AI, said in the announcement that his company ran Mercury 3 inside its production web-agent harness against frontier models on 50 live Mind2Web navigation tasks, where Mercury 3 completed 50% of them, which he described as significantly more than GPT-6.1-Sol, using the same token volume and the same number of agent steps at a fraction of the per-token cost.

Michael Tong, co-founder and CTO of General Learning, known as RevisionDojo, said Mercury 3 let the tutoring company give every student instant feedback “without giving up reasoning,” with hints, marked answers, and definitions returning in about a second at q...
news.content_snippet: Nvidia is in advanced talks to acquire Inception, a two-year-old startup that develops a type of AI that aims to perform faster …
news.summary_en: Nvidia is in advanced talks to acquire diffusion-based LLM developer Inception for over $500 million, including earnouts. Inception recently launched Mercury 3, a model utilizing diffusion scaling laws to outperform autoregressive models like GPT-6.1-Sol in specific benchmarks, achieving speeds exceeding 1,000 tokens per second.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 英伟达正处于收购Diffusion架构大模型初创公司Inception的深度谈判阶段，交易金额预计超过5亿美元并包含额外收益权对赌协议。Inception近期发布的Mercury 3模型凭借扩散架构，实现了在特定推理任务中超越自回归模型（如GPT-6.1-Sol）的性能表现，且推理速度达到每秒1068 token。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Nvidia is in advanced talks to acquire diffusion-based LLM developer Inception for over $500 million, including earnouts. Inception recently launched Mercury 3, a model utilizing diffusion scaling laws to outperform autoregressive models like GPT-6.1-Sol in specific benchmarks, achieving speeds exceeding 1,000 tokens per second.

elements_zh.where: 企业兼并与收购（M&A）市场

elements_zh.why: 验证了扩散模型在处理复杂任务时具备与自回归模型竞争的扩展定律，且推理效率具有显著差异化优势

elements_en.what: Acquisition deal over $500M involving Mercury 3 technology integration
elements_en.why: Validation of diffusion scaling laws competing with autoregressive models and superior inference efficiency

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 此次收购标志着英伟达正加速通过构建技术防火墙来对抗Transformer架构在推理侧的效率瓶颈。Inception验证的扩散模型扩展定律若能整合入英伟达的软硬一体架构中，将直接威胁现有自回归模型的市场定价基准，并为特定实时代理场景提供远超传统方案的低延迟算力支持。
ai_analysis.insight_en: This acquisition signals Nvidia's strategic push to mitigate the inference bottlenecks of Transformer architectures by diversifying into diffusion-based LLMs. Integrating Inception's validated scaling laws into Nvidia's vertical stack could disrupt current autoregressive pricing models and provide a decisive low-latency advantage for real-time agentic workflows.

news.title: Sources: National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is leaving now to let the White House get a successor confirmed before Democrats take the Senate in January (Axios)
news.title_en: Sources: National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is leaving now to let the White House get a successor confirmed before Democrats take the Senate in January (Axios)

inline_images.caption: White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross (left), who is leaving his post, with President Trump during an Oval Office event on June 22. Photo: Andrew
inline_images.alt: White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross (left), who is leaving his post, with President

news.author: Axios
news.article_content:
White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross is leaving his post, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: Cairncross did not want to serve another two years and is leaving now to give the White House time to secure Senate confirmation before Democrats take control in January, two sources said.

The background: Cairncross leads the Office of the National Cyber Director, which coordinates cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government.

Case in point: He held technical meetings with Anthropic leaders over the summer after Commerce Department export controls effectively scrubbed the company's models from the internet.

Catch up quick: Cairncross brought experience in Republican politics and national security, having worked with the intelligence community and dealt with cyber threats at the Republican National Committee.

The big picture: The latest turnover in cyber personnel comes as the country grapples with critical infrastructure outages and increasingly powerful AI poised to empower cyber defenders and hackers alike.

What we're watching: Trump is also filling other key cyber positions.

news.summary_en: US National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is stepping down to provide a transition window for his successor to be confirmed by the Senate before Democrats gain control in January. As the head of the Office of the National Cyber Director, Cairncross led federal cybersecurity strategy and notably directed technical reviews of AI firms like Anthropic following commerce-led export control implementations.

news.title: Apple is hiring engineers to build its own AI agent
news.title_en: Apple is hiring engineers to build its own AI agent
news.author: Emma Roth
news.article_content:
Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That’s according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which says Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant.

An AI agent from Apple would put the iPhonemaker in the running to compete with the likes of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Duet, and Google’s Tasks. Muse, ChatGPT, and Perplexity can already take control of a computer through their Mac apps, while Google just started letting Gemini do the same.

Apple began rolling out its AI-upgraded Siri in September, which you can use to ask questions about what’s on your screen, as well as perform actions across apps. It looks like Apple is planning to give Siri more agentic capabilities, as a report from Bloomberg suggests the company could add the ability to rotate and crop images in Photos, or organize Safari tabs. This lines up with the company’s new job listing, which says the engineer will work closely with teams across its Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models divisions.

“People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service,” the job listing says. “We’re building AI agents that can do the same… These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.”

With its upcoming iOS 27.3 update, Apple is also giving developers the ability to integrate Siri AI into “all apps.” This is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview and will eventually allow Siri to perform tasks across a wider range of apps.

news.title_zh: 苹果招募工程师研发自主AI代理
news.summary_zh: 苹果发布高级工程管理职位，旨在开发能够跨应用操作、编写代码及浏览网页的自主AI代理系统

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 苹果公司通过发布“Agentic AI”高级工程经理招聘启事，明确将其研发重心从现有的Siri被动式功能转向具备跨应用交互、代码调试及自主决策能力的代理系统。该项目将协同Siri团队、UI框架部门及Apple Foundation Models部门，旨在打破系统内单应用操作的局限，实现跨设备、跨平台的复杂任务规划与自动化处理。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Apple is pivoting its AI strategy by recruiting for a 'Proactive, Agentic AI' engineering lead to develop autonomous systems capable of cross-app interaction, code debugging, and complex task planning. The initiative, integrating teams from Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models, aims to move beyond static voice commands toward an autonomous agent environment capable of multi-step execution across devices.

elements_zh.who: 苹果公司（Apple）及其AI研发部门
elements_zh.where: 企业内部招聘与系统架构规划
elements_zh.what: 招募研发负责人以构建自主AI代理，实现跨浏览器、代码编辑、终端指令及应用服务的自动执行
elements_zh.why: 应对Meta、Google及OpenAI在代理式AI领域的快速市场扩张，通过端侧隐私优势巩固生态护城河

elements_en.who: Apple and its core AI engineering divisions
elements_en.where: Internal R&D and platform architecture roadmap
elements_en.what: Recruiting leadership to develop autonomous AI agents for cross-app execution, web browsing, and code generation
elements_en.why: To counter the rapid market penetration of AI agents from competitors and leverage Apple's privacy-centric hardware integration

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 苹果的逻辑是利用macOS和iOS的底层权限优势，将AI代理锚定在“隐私合规”的护城河内，以对抗Meta等竞品激进的UI劫持式代理技术。此举本质上是在重塑操作系统的人机交互范式，即由用户主动指令转向AI模型作为“系统操作者”，这将对应用生态的入口价值产生深远挤压。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Apple is leveraging its OS-level permission control to build a 'privacy-first' moat for AI agents, countering the UI-overtaking approaches used by competitors. This marks a paradigm shift in human-computer interaction, transforming AI models from mere assistants into autonomous system operators, which effectively challenges the traditional interface value of third-party applications.

news.title: Apple Is Working on AI Agent for Device Control, Apps, Browsing and Coding
news.title_en: Apple Is Working on AI Agent for Device Control, Apps, Browsing and Coding
news.author: Bloomberg
news.article_content:

news.title: A brief history of Nvidia’s recent stock fluctuations
news.title_en: A brief history of Nvidia’s recent stock fluctuations
news.author: Ellen Thomas
news.article_content:
“We’ve got this,” Colette Kress, interim CEO of Nvidia, said Tuesday night as she closed out the embattled chip company’s third quarter earnings call.

By Thursday, the company’s stock price was hovering at around $150 per share, a nearly 40 percent drop from its all-time high on October 6th, and wiping out a brief post-earnings pop on Tuesday night. Meanwhile, Wall Street was paying up for one of Nvidia’s biggest customers as Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut at $111.50 per share — 34 percent higher than expected.

Looking at the earnings report numbers alone, Nvidia had a blockbuster quarter. Q3 revenue more than doubled from the same period last year up to total $115.8 billion, driven by data center revenue that was up 110 percent and exceeding Wall Street expectations. Nearly $20 billion in revenue came from the highly anticipated Vera Rubin platform, which shipped during the quarter, becoming the “fastest product ramp in company history,” Kress told investors.

“Our momentum is real,” Kress said. “With the market-leading multiyear roadmap, supply agreements extending through to the end of the decade, and sustainable demand, we are well positioned to accelerate Nvidia’s leadership position.”

But investors are stilltrying to reconcile Nvidia’s stellar recent financial performance and position as a central pillar in the AI economy with serious concerns over its future.

The company’s stock has taken a stunning tumble in recent weeks. Fueled first by a broader market sell-off of chip stocks amid concerns about the AI bubble, the stock took another blow following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, according to US intelligence sources cited by The New York Times.

Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s newly appointed chairman of the board, told investors on the call Tuesday that the company “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and has already tapped an executive search firm to help find a replacement. Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and has led the company ever since — famously without a succession plan — has become essentially inseparable from it in the eyes of Wall Street and the media. But while Huang may not be ready to let go, posting on X this week that he’d be “honored” to be reinstated as CEO, Nvidia’s executive suite seems ready to move on.

It has been a tumultuous two and a half weeks for Nvidia.

The report centered on his “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company and one of Nvidia’s clients. paragraphs: “We’ve got this,” Colette Kress, interim CEO of Nvidia, said Tuesday night as she closed out the embattled chip company’s third quarter earnings call.

By Thursday, the company’s stock price was hovering at around $150 per share, a nearly 40 percent drop from its all-time high on October 6th, and wiping out a brief post-earnings pop on Tuesday night. Meanwhile, Wall Street was paying up for one of Nvidia’s biggest customers as Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut at $111.50 per share — 34 percent higher than expected.

Looking at the earnings report numbers alone, Nvidia had a blockbuster quarter. Q3 revenue more than doubled from the same period last year up to total $115.8 billion, driven by data center revenue that was up 110 percent and exceeding Wall Street expectations. Nearly $20 billion in revenue came from the highly anticipated Vera Rubin platform, which shipped during the quarter, becoming the “fastest product ramp in company history,” Kress told investors.

“Our momentum is real,” Kress said. “With the market-leading multiyear roadmap, supply agreements extending through to the end of the decade, and sustainable demand, we are well positioned to accelerate Nvidia’s leadership position.”
But investors are stilltrying to reconcile Nvidia’s stellar recent financial performance and position as a central pillar in the AI economy with serious concerns over its future.

The company’s stock has taken a stunning tumble in recent weeks. Fueled first by a broader market sell-off of chip stocks amid concerns about the AI bubble, the stock took another blow following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, according to US intelligence sources cited by The New York Times.

Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s newly appointed chairman of the board, told investors on the call Tuesday that the company “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and has already tapped an executive search firm to help find a replacement. Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and has led the company ever since — famously without a succession plan — has become essentially inseparable from it in the eyes of Wall Street and the media. But while Huang may not be ready to let go, posting on X this week that he’d be “honored” to be reinstated as CEO, Nvidia’s executive suite seems ready to move on.
It has been a tumultuous two and a half weeks for Nvidia.

On October 29th, The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies believed Jensen Huang to be the target of a Chinese espionage plot. The report centered on his “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company and one of Nvidia’s clients. Nvidia initially contested the report, adding that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang “are not unusual or unexpected.”

Nvidia’s stock seemingly remained unaffected by the reports, at least at first. The share price closed at $213.66 on October 29th, down just 0.8 percent from the previous day. (Julian Barnes, one of the reporters on the story, later commented, “I will confess I was kind of surprised that the world’s initial reaction to our October story was a bit muted.”) The stock closed at a 4 percent drop the next day as the entire Nasdaq fell 2.9 percent, the worst single-day decline since June.

The stock continued to fall through Wednesday, November 4th, the day after the blue wave swept the midterms, stoking fears on Wall Street that the new class of Democratic governors in key states like Texas would slow down data center construction. On Thursday, November 5th, Nvidia’s stock fell 9.2 percent, its largest single-day drop in at least a year. But chip stocks began to recover the next day, and by close on Friday, November 6th, Nvidia was back up 2.8 percent to a share price of $186.64.

Then all hell broke loose. On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang sent a company-wide memo to Nvidia staff in which he apologized for engaging in an extramarital affair. The memo coincided with the opening of an independent investigation by Nvidia’s board into Huang’s alleged misconduct and whether company secrets or national security had been compromised. Huang said he would cooperate fully with the investigation. By the opening bell on Monday, November 9th, Nvidia shares had tumbled 7 percent and trading volume surged past its three-month average as investors reacted to the memo. After a brief rebound, the stock continued to oscillate the next day, as more details of Jensen Huang and Alice Huang’s relationship emerged. By the time the market closed on Tuesday, November 10th, Nvidia shares were down to $168.89, nearly 10 percent below the closing price on the last day of 2025.

The stock rebounded slightly on Wednesday, November 11th, as investors prepared for Nvidia’s third quarter earnings call, scheduled for the following Tuesday, November 17th. By Wednesday night, however, shares had plunged yet again as media reports circulated that Nvidia’s board was considering ousting Huang, and other reports emerged detailing a second alleged affair, this time between Huang and an Nvidia employee.

Nvidia announced Huang’s departure on the morning of Thursday, November 12th, sending the company’s shares falling nearly 14 percent at the open. It closed at just a 4.3 percent dip. The intraday low of $148.80 per share was its lowest price in a year.

On December 1st, Jensen Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence Committee for transcribed interviews. Nvidia’s general counsel will do the same on December 2nd.

Retail investors have already seized the opportunity to buy the dip. In the first 30 minutes of trading on Thursday, November 12th, retail investors bought $111 million of Nvidia shares in the largest-ever first half-hour of opening for the stock, Bloomberg reported, citing Vanda Research.
They might be onto something.
Nvidia’s average price target is $232.59, with the lowest estimate at $130 and the highest at $350, according to an analysis of analyst projections over the last three months by Google Finance.
Nearly two-thirds of those analysts issued a “Buy” rating for Nvidia in the last three months. Of those, all 30 reiterated that rating post-earnings.
The stock closed at $145.98 on Thursday, a new 52-week low.

Then again, numbers are the core basis for stock market ratings, and numbers may not be Nvidia’s problem right now. It’s everything else — the leadership vacuum, upcoming congressional testimony, regulatory uncertainty, broader questions about neocloud customer financing and sales to China — that will continue to impact the stock in the coming weeks.

Brian Barrett: All right look, if you picked up your phone at any point in last week to look at the news, if you went to wired.com at any point last week or anywhere on social media, you were hit with news that something somewhere had an outage.
Leah Feiger: Brian, everything is broken.

Leah Feiger: Every single thing is broken.

We're going to list off some of the biggest ones, OK? Last Thursday, Microsoft had an outage in Outlook and Teams that was about 24 hours, which is incredibly long for those services to be out when the whole world basically depends on them to communicate. The next day, Friday, the FAA had a ground stop for the entire country, only the second time that has happened since 9/11, and it was the longest one since then. It was for more than four hours. Then on Monday, everyone said that their banks no longer worked. It turns out to be JP Morgan Chase specifically had a problem, but because banks are all counterparties to each other, every bank had an issue. If one bank had an issue, that same day, United delayed more than a hundred flights for a separate issue. Then on Tuesday, the NSA's classified internal network went down and just for good measure, an internal update also knocked out iCloud and Apple Pay for not quite as long, not quite as dramatically, but throw it on the pile. Now I want to be clear, every single one of these companies and agencies and organizations has said the incidents were not cyberattacks. It was not some combination of a ruthless AI agent and Iranian hackers. There's no evidence that any of these clustered tech failures were even related aside from the bank thing, which is self-contained in the banking industry, but that hasn't stopped people from being suspicious, trying to find a through line, and I think getting on their conspiracy horses. And Sophie, you've been riding one at the front of the battle.
Sophie Kleeman: Yes, I sure have.
Brian Barrett: Yeah. How are you taking all of this in so I can debunk it?
Sophie Kleeman: OK. So I would like to say first off that I do think this has sort of trickled down into people who don't follow this super closely.
Leah Feiger: I mean, it had to. This was your emails, this was your banking, these were your flights.
Sophie Kleeman: Right. Everyone's talking about this.
Leah Feiger: This is it.

Sophie Kleeman: To give you two very, very, very distinct examples, yesterday my fantasy football group chat blew up because someone was like, "Hey guys who follow this, and who are paying attention, are we under attack?" And Brian, you'll be proud of me. I actually said you should read wired.com for the answer to that.
Brian Barrett: Good job, Sophie.
Leah Feiger: She did not say, "Yes, go to the bunkers." Which I know is what you wanted to say.
Sophie Kleeman: It is what I wanted to say.

Leah Feiger: Look, I will say though, I get that inclination. These are so many public services that everyone has really just taken for granted, not only to work, but to help us function in our day-to-day lives. I talked to friends who were like, "Oh yeah, I just had a day and a half off of work basically, and then could not pay my rent." It was everything.

Brian Barrett: And there are people who are doing doomsday prepping at Costco now. I've had multiple group chats where people, even when I've told them, "Hey, it's actually fine," they are still prepping their bunkers. I think it's instructive. I have covered outages for a long time at WIRED because I think they're fascinating because they affect so many people, and they have such mundane causes usually. So I want to talk through a couple of things and what happened. Just for any listeners who are still worried about it, they all have very distinct things. The Microsoft Outlook issue was actually ... I love this one. It was a fix that was deployed in July. They basically made an update in July, propagated it out, but was not triggered until last week. Something else happened.
Sophie Kleeman: Do we know what that something else is? I'm just asking questions.

Brian Barrett: Iranian hackers. No, they've done a shorter postmortem. They're going to do a longer postmortem. The gist of it was they pushed this thing out and then it propagated out through the whole network and then they had another update. They stepped on the landmine and everything went boom, and it took a while to correct. For the FAA, when air traffic control went down, and Aarian Marshall, who covers transportation mobility for us here at WIRED, was very early to say this doesn't seem like hackers. There was a lot of suspicion there because the FAA just the day before had rolled out an AI system to help with air traffic control. The difference is that system's more about data, and about where planes are going and what they're doing. The system that was affected, the problem on Friday, was that people couldn't talk to each other. It was a comms issue. And that tied back to old, old, old fiber equipment that a company called L3Harris maintains. They were trying to push an update on Friday afternoon, which you never do. That's the crazy part to me is that they were trying to push—
Leah Feiger: It's the perfect time.
Sophie Kleeman: Yeah.
Brian Barrett: Push an update to production on a Friday, a couple weeks before Thanksgiving? Crazy stuff.

Leah Feiger: And then I mean the rest was all the same too, right Brian? Chase blamed a software bug in their own hardware. United said it was a technology related issue. Sophie Kleeman: At the same time.

Sophie Kleeman: Email season.

Leah Feiger: But it is understandable that everyone went straight to the hackers, straight to AI overlords because we've actually been having a not small amount of those examples. If you had told me that this was another Hugging Face incident, I would've been like, yep. Alright. Sounds good.
Sophie Kleeman: You're like, yeah, that sounds right.

Brian Barrett: Well, and Leah too, I think what doesn't help, there's the political dimension here too, because Markwayne Mullin can tell me everything's fine, all he wants. I don't necessarily buy anything from him.
Sophie Kleeman: I don't believe him.
Brian Barrett: Right. I inherently, this administration has no credibility. So in these moments, what do we do?

Leah Feiger: I have to shout out our podcast producer right now. Obviously we are sitting here with a list of notes about all of this and I just quickly looked at it and one tab line was, also people don't trust the government.
Sophie Kleeman: Incredible.

Leah Feiger: Which is, yeah, that is the situation right now. That is perhaps the most succinct, accurate way to push this, which is there was just a massive referendum a few weeks ago. Dems are coming in, guns blazing, and everything is breaking right before that happens. I get it.

Sophie Kleeman: I'm the devil's advocate here, right? I was the person last week where I was like, we're all going to die. We're under attack. This is crazy. This is all happening at the same time. I think people are quick to blame AI for things because they don't like it, they don't understand it, they are scared of it, and the companies who are selling it are not doing a great job of selling their product in ways that make people want to sort of feel good about themselves. But the second point is that it was AI, right? It was just the flip side of it. It was like, these companies are deploying these incredibly advanced systems to find vulnerabilities, to find issues within their very complex and in some cases old systems and they're finding it and then they're patching it all at the same time. And that's what I think that reporting has suggested that's what we're seeing.

Brian Barrett: This goes back to Anthropic's Mythos model, which is very good at cybersecurity. You might remember it from such news headlines as Anthropic gets banned from the Pentagon and other stupid moments in AI history. Mythos is very, very good at cybersecurity. Anthropic gave access to a limited number, actually a decent number of people who control sensitive information, governments, organizations, companies, and those companies have since been using it to identify bugs that they couldn't find otherwise. Sending patches at a huge rate, and the more complicated the bug, the more patches trying to push out at the same time, the more likely something is going to break. And I think that's what we're seeing here. So yeah, AI plays a role, but in some ways you can think of this as companies trying to get ahead of the hacking version of this. They're doing this because otherwise, in a few months, someone's going to actually say, oh, we can break into the air traffic control system, shut it down ourselves.

There's an interesting look, at least for me, of the accountability of it all, of is this possible? I guess this is possible. This shouldn't be possible.

Sophie Kleeman: I'm fascinated by this. And Brian, I would love to know what you think is going on here because I sort of though the sharks would be circling in a way, or I thought that they would not want to touch this with a 10-foot pole kind of thing. I mean, I understand that Jensen is just such a sort of crucial part of this ecosystem and Nvidia is such a crucial part of this ecosystem. Brian Barrett: Oh, because I think that they all see a little bit of themselves in him.
Leah Feiger: He's one of their own.

We talked about this before, it's the idea of separating the art from the artist, but applied to real allegedly scummy behavior, like having sex with a direct report and lying to your board of directors about it. They've got customers that don't have anywhere else to turn, and it will be a long time before they do. They may not be as essential a pillar to the US economy and the industry in the long run. And this issue became the entire issue this past week because of Nvidia, because Alice Huang was an executive at one of these companies, Megaspeed. WIRED senior correspondent Hugo Lowell has been reporting on what the administration's response has been throughout all of this. And it's been really interesting, honestly, which is for as much as Trump and co are like, "We have to be ahead of China. This is the whole thing. We can't slow down. We can't have guardrails. We have to beat China." There's also been this undercurrent of figuring out how you cooperate, how you're still making money without stifling innovation. This has played out into disputes within Trump's own cabinet. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent versus Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. I have loved the drama of it all.
Sophie Kleeman: The girls are fighting.

Leah Feiger: The girls are fighting. But frankly, for as much as Bessent spent the last week throwing Lutnick entirely under the rug, it kind of turns out, and Hugo found, that Trump has been really playing that middle and siding with Lutnick in a lot of this. So this new rule is going to be really interesting. I'm very curious about it getting enforced. I'm curious about how it's going to also be talked about and communicated this week on the ground actually in China. Hugo's newsletter that published Wednesday night gets into this, and basically what officials have told him quietly is that there probably isn't going to be a lot of movement on AI as Trump arrives, really because of the Nvidia scandal, because there has been so much consternation of quote, unquote Chinese spies everywhere. And this conversation is a little bit at a standstill. So new rule, conversations happening, maybe no results. I don't know. Is that politics as usual? Perhaps.

Brian Barrett: I have a couple questions. One, this is a dumb one, I'm sorry, but we just heard Donald Trump saying, when asked about outages, that if you're big, then people will go for you, even though that has nothing to do with what's going on. So my question, Leah, the eternal question with Donald Trump, how much do we think he actually knows or cares about any of this versus whoever was in the room with him last has told him a thing that sounds good?

Leah Feiger: Oh, I think that's a huge part of it. Ultimately, and I should have this tattooed on my forehead, which is that similar rules to these already existed. They existed in the Biden era. Trump rolled them back in 2025. Again, unclear how much of that context is memorable to the administration or to Trump himself. But I think the underlying current, really for him, for as far as we've been able to understand from his public statements and his private ones that people have been able to report out, is that he wants the US to be competitive. Fist on table, be competitive. Whether that means we're selling chips or not selling chips, they're not very complicated thoughts. I'm sorry to say. I don't know how else to put it other than I'm not sure that the minutia is that interesting to him. And frankly, the minutia is barely interesting to the rest of us.
Sophie Kleeman: It's deeply unsexy. It's deeply unsexy.

Sophie Kleeman: I mean, my question too, not to put on my conspiracy theory hat again, but I think-
Brian Barrett: Dit it.
Leah Feiger: This is when we unveil you as our ... This is why you're here.
Sophie Kleeman: Resident conspiracy theorist. I mean, so the reporting about this, it was a little bit hedged. It was like they are moving toward closing a loophole.

They have to appease the anti-China hawks in the party while also having to work with the richest nation around. And so it's a very tricky balance.

Brian Barrett: One last politics thing to mention, just because it's significant. It has nothing to do with export controls. news.title: Intuit to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion
news.title_en: Intuit to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion
news.author: Jordan Novet
news.article_content:
Tax software maker Intuit said Thursday that it has agreed to sell marketing subsidiary Mailchimp to Italian technology consolidator Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion in cash and stock. The deal is set to close in early 2027, according to a statement.

The sale is a costly retreat for Intuit, which paid $12 billion for Mailchimp in 2021 in a push beyond its core tax and accounting businesses. Five years later, the software maker is unloading the email-marketing company for less than one-third of that price after Mailchimp became a drag on its overall revenue growth.

The deal is the latest instance of Bending Spoons picking up a once promising technology asset. The company bought productivity software startup Airtable in September for 10% of what it was once worth.

The Bending Spoons portfolio also contains AOL, Brightcove, Eventbrite, Evernote, Meetup, Vimeo, and WeTransfer.

In August Intuit started running Mailchimp as a distinct operating segment. The move was meant to give investors more transparency as the company tried to manage the unit for profitability, Sandeep Aujla, Intuit's finance chief, said at a September company briefing.

Also on Thursday, Intuit announced stronger-than-expected earnings and revenue for its fiscal first quarter, which ended on Oct. 31. The company reported $2.91 in adjusted earnings per share on $4.35 billion in revenue. Analysts polled by LSEG were looking for $2.70 per share and $4.31 billion in revenue.

While Intuit's revenue increased 12% year over year, Mailchimp revenue declined 1% to $313 million. Analysts polled by StreetAccount had expected $314.4 million.

Management called for $22.88 to $23.12 in adjusted earnings per share for the 2027 fiscal year, with $23.081 billion to $23.365 billion in revenue. Analysts polled by LSEG had predicted $23.62 in adjusted earnings per share on $23.43 billion in revenue. Intuit shares tumbled 15% in extended trading.

The company said Mailchimp should produce $1.256 billion to $1.266 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue, which would be down 1% to flat year over year. In August Aujla said Intuit anticipated Mailchimp's higher effective prices offsetting increased client churn. Mailchimp was founded in 2001. Rivals include Klaviyo, which went public in 2023.

Berkshire Hathaway invested $600 million in Bending Spoons when the acquirer went public in July, and in October Bending Spoons said Berkshire invested another $330 million.

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 此交易标志着Intuit从“跨领域扩张”重回“核心财务软件”的战略收缩，暴露了SaaS领域盲目并购在跨生态整合时的价值损耗。Bending Spoons采取的“低价吸纳存量资产”模式虽能维持财报短期账面增长，但其能否在存量市场中通过精细化运营遏制产品生命周期衰减仍存在巨大的财务风险。
ai_analysis.insight_en: This transaction signals Intuit's strategic retrenchment back to its core tax software business, exposing the value destruction inherent in cross-domain M&A within the SaaS sector. Michael LoSapio, the chief information security officer at the data analytics firm Palantir, provided only high-level answers to members of the Senate Homeland Security Committee who asked him how he would restore CISA’s ability to combat cyber threats after two years of Trump administration cuts.

“I believe CISA is one of the only agencies in the government that plays a defensive cyber role in our nation,” LoSapio told Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., who will chair the homeland-security panel in the next session of Congress.

CISA’s “sole purpose is to provide resources [and] information to the defenders of state, local, and private entities for the purpose of cyber defense,” LoSapio continued. “If confirmed, I intend to bring together the community and the national labs to help collaborate and coordinate and to give defenders the tools they need to defend their networks.”

LoSapio also described CISA as “the cybersecurity version of the 911 system” because of its role in responding to significant cyber incidents.

But LoSapio, whose firm has extensive and controversial connections to the Trump administration, refused to weigh in on the administration’s downsizing of CISA, which has included mass layoffs and significant changes to the agency’s programs and services.

“I can’t comment on the current state of CISA, because I’m not inside today,” he told Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich.

When Slotkin pressed LoSapio on whether he would support the Trump administration’s proposed $385 million cut to CISA’s budget, LoSapio again dodged the question.

“I'm going to get involved and understand where the gaps are,” he said, “and I will come back to this committee with a gap analysis.”

Slotkin said LoSapio was too afraid of angering Trump to be an effective CISA director.

“You should be able to say clearly, there’s increasing threat, therefore we need increasing resources to deal with it,” she said, “and the fact that you can’t say that means that you’re more worried about the political ramifications than you are about the national security of the country.”

“I don’t necessarily believe more money means more security,” LoSapio responded. “I believe spending money on the right solutions in the right ways actually decreases risk.”

news.article_content:
Few things could generate more buzz for a small restaurant than a visit from Jensen Huang. In recent years, the former Nvidia CEO became known for dining out at street markets and hole-in-the-wall noodle joints across Asia, drawing huge crowds of fans and photographers wherever he went.

But after Huang resigned last week amid revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, some of the food vendors he helped put on the map are wondering whether their most famous customer is still good for business. In Taiwan, where Huang was born and his dining habits have long been a spectator sport, many say they aren't ready to turn against their hometown hero.

Tu Chang-chun, the owner of Ice World, a shaved-ice shop in Taipei, describes Huang as friendly, the kind of person who puts others around him at ease. His impression of the billionaire hasn’t changed since he learned of his affair with Alice Huang, a businesswoman accused of spying for China.

“It’s not as if he killed someone or set something on fire. Why blow it all out of proportion?” Tu said on Monday evening, standing beneath the yellow lights of his stall at Linjiang Street Night Market. “Now, a lot of foreigners walk past, see my sign, and laugh. People just love kicking someone when they’re down.”

At the entrance of his shop, Tu continues to proudly display a photo of Huang posing with him and his wife. “I think he’s such a warm and approachable person,” Tu added. “Why are people treating him this way?”

Jensen Huang has visited this shaved ice stall at Taipei’s Linjiang Street Night Market three times since 2023.

Tu says that Huang has visited his shop three times since 2023, and he always orders the same thing: mango shaved ice with tangyuan (sticky rice balls). The dessert, a blend of tropical fruit and condensed milk, is popular in Taipei’s bustling night markets, especially among first-time visitors to the island.

“When he came in for shaved ice, he would spend half an hour eating a single bowl,” recalled Tu. “Whenever someone came up to take a photo with him, he got right up. He’s not pretentious.”

At a tofu pudding shop near Ningxia Night Market in western Taipei, photos of Huang remain on display alongside those of other prominent technology figures who have visited, including Morris Chang, the founder of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC). The store manager, Hsieh, defended the shop’s decision to keep them up.

“I don’t think this changes the fact that he’s a very successful businessman,” Hsieh said of Huang’s affairs with Alice Huang and other women. “Having an affair is a private matter.”

paragraphs: Few things could generate more buzz for a small restaurant than a visit from Jensen Huang. In recent years, the former Nvidia CEO became known for dining out at street markets and hole-in-the-wall noodle joints across Asia, drawing huge crowds of fans and photographers wherever he went.

But after Huang resigned last week amid revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, some of the food vendors he helped put on the map are wondering whether their most famous customer is still good for business. In Taiwan, where Huang was born and his dining habits have long been a spectator sport, many say they aren't ready to turn against their hometown hero.

“It’s not as if he killed someone or set something on fire. Why blow it all out of proportion?” Tu said on Monday evening, standing beneath the yellow lights of his stall at Linjiang Street Night Market. “Now, a lot of foreigners walk past, see my sign, and laugh. People just love kicking someone when they’re down.”

At the entrance of his shop, Tu continues to proudly display a photo of Huang posing with him and his wife. “I think he’s such a warm and approachable person,” Tu added. “Why are people treating him this way?”
Jensen Huang has visited this shaved ice stall at Taipei’s Linjiang Street Night Market three times since 2023.

Tu says that Huang has visited his shop three times since 2023, and he always orders the same thing: mango shaved ice with tangyuan (sticky rice balls). The dessert, a blend of tropical fruit and condensed milk, is popular in Taipei’s bustling night markets, especially among first-time visitors to the island.
“When he came in for shaved ice, he would spend half an hour eating a single bowl,” recalled Tu. “Whenever someone came up to take a photo with him, he got right up. He’s not pretentious.”

At a tofu pudding shop near Ningxia Night Market in western Taipei, photos of Huang remain on display alongside those of other prominent technology figures who have visited, including Morris Chang, the founder of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC). The store manager, Hsieh, defended the shop’s decision to keep them up.
“I don’t think this changes the fact that he’s a very successful businessman,” Hsieh said of Huang’s affairs with Alice Huang and other women. “Having an affair is a private matter.”

Hsieh, who agreed to be identified only by his surname for privacy reasons, said that Huang had visited the shop four times over the past few years, and on each occasion he seemed friendly and down-to-earth.
Owner Tu Chang-chun said he has no plans to take down photos Jensen Huang visiting his shaved-ice shop.

In Taiwan, Huang’s culinary indulgences extended well beyond street food. He frequented some of Taipei’s most exclusive restaurants, where he hosted technology executives for what became known in the local press as “Trillion-Dollar Banquets,” a reference to the attendees’ combined net worth of more than 1 trillion New Taiwan dollars.

The dinners often drew crowds of journalists and photographers hoping to catch a glimpse of Huang and his guests. The intense media attention helps explain why so many photographs and videos of Huang with Alice Huang were captured in Taiwan. Restaurant owners, meanwhile, welcomed the publicity, often proudly displaying photographs of themselves with Huang inside their establishments.

The Taiwanese tea chain 19 Tea House launched a new drink this week, giving it a name that pokes fun at Huang’s alleged “womanizing” ways. According to the chain, the drink combines osmanthus-infused honey with fresh lemon, offering a blend of fragrant floral notes and sweet-and-tangy citrus flavors.

Support for Huang in Taiwan has also extended far beyond the restaurants he frequented. On Monday evening, Taipei 101, the island’s iconic skyscraper just blocks from one of Huang’s favorite night markets, lit up with messages of support for the former Nvidia CEO, including “Taiwan ♡ Jensen,” “Family ♡ Friendship,” “Thrive Together,” and “Taiwan AI Build Future Together.”

Tech industry figures who supported the initiative told Taiwan’s state-run Central News Agency that the illumination campaign was intended to “help restore Jensen Huang’s reputation,” urging the public not to “kick him when he's down, but instead offer warmth and support during the autumn and winter.”

news.title: Man hired by Russia spied on Silicon Valley tech and defense company, feds say
news.title_en: Man hired by Russia spied on Silicon Valley tech and defense company, feds say
news.author: Dan Goodin
news.article_content:
A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley company that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its western neighbor.

Igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors said Wednesday. He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. An affidavit filed in the case referred to the employee as FEMP1, short for female employee, and said the event left her “in a state of emotional distress.”

### Evasive and irregular turns

“FEMP1 made evasive and irregular turns, took back roads, and turned into a grocery store parking lot where D’IU continued aggressively following her vehicle,” an FBI special agent wrote. “D’IU followed FEMP1 through U-turns, illegal left turns, and ran a red light to stay with FEMP1 for nearly thirty miles. FEMP1 called 911 while driving and was instructed to drive directly to San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) Mission Station. Near SFPD Mission Station, FEMP1 flagged an SFPD patrol vehicle and reported the incident. D’IU left once FEMP1 made contact with the patrol vehicle.”

When police later questioned D’iu about the incident, the defendant allegedly said he saw a woman get into a car and thought she was “beautiful.” He then told the investigators that he followed her because he “wanted to ask her out on a date.”

Prosecutors didn’t name the company, but both Reuters and Bloomberg, citing unnamed people with knowledge of the case, identified it as Palantir. Ars is unable to confirm that reporting. Palantir representatives didn’t respond to an email seeking confirmation.

D’iu allegedly entered the US unlawfully in the summer of 2026 after being recruited by someone over Telegram. Prosecutors said the party gave D’iu a clandestine assignment to target employees of a large technology and defense company. D’iu received instructions, equipment, and financial support along with information that his work was on behalf of “the motherland.” His instructions were to collect information about the company because it was supplying weapons for use against Russian forces in Ukraine.

Prosecutors said D’iu traveled from Istanbul, Turkey, to Mexico City in June. He then crossed the border into the US and was instructed to buy laptops, cell phones, wireless networking equipment, and remote access software. Igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors said Wednesday. He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. An affidavit filed in the case referred to the employee as FEMP1, short for female employee, and said the event left her “in a state of emotional distress.”
### Evasive and irregular turns

“FEMP1 made evasive and irregular turns, took back roads, and turned into a grocery store parking lot where D’IU continued aggressively following her vehicle,” an FBI special agent wrote. “D’IU followed FEMP1 through U-turns, illegal left turns, and ran a red light to stay with FEMP1 for nearly thirty miles. FEMP1 called 911 while driving and was instructed to drive directly to San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) Mission Station. Near SFPD Mission Station, FEMP1 flagged an SFPD patrol vehicle and reported the incident. D’IU left once FEMP1 made contact with the patrol vehicle.”

When police later questioned D’iu about the incident, the defendant allegedly said he saw a woman get into a car and thought she was “beautiful.” He then told the investigators that he followed her because he “wanted to ask her out on a date.”

Prosecutors didn’t name the company, but both Reuters and Bloomberg, citing unnamed people with knowledge of the case, identified it as Palantir. Ars is unable to confirm that reporting. Palantir representatives didn’t respond to an email seeking confirmation.

D’iu allegedly entered the US unlawfully in the summer of 2026 after being recruited by someone over Telegram. Prosecutors said the party gave D’iu a clandestine assignment to target employees of a large technology and defense company. D’iu received instructions, equipment, and financial support along with information that his work was on behalf of “the motherland.” His instructions were to collect information about the company because it was supplying weapons for use against Russian forces in Ukraine.

Prosecutors said D’iu traveled from Istanbul, Turkey, to Mexico City in June. He then crossed the border into the US and was instructed to buy laptops, cell phones, wireless networking equipment, and remote access software. Besides instructions to monitor company employees at the coffee shop, D’iu’s orders also included positioning his laptop at certain locations near the company so it could be remotely accessed in an attempt to collect information from company employees nearby.

D’iu allegedly obtained fraudulent identification documents to conceal his identity as he conducted his activities. The documents included a falsified California ID card, an altered US passport, and a Social Security card bearing the assumed name of “Hugo Landry Johns.” The passport was allegedly an authentic US passport that originally had been issued to someone elsewhere in the country. It was modified to display D’iu’s photograph and assumed identity.

D’iu was arrested on October 30 and remains in custody. He is charged with one count of Conspiracy to Act as an Agent of a Foreign Government, one count of Acting as an Agent of a Foreign Government Without Notice to the Attorney General, and one count of Interstate Stalking. If convicted for Acting as an Agent of a Foreign Government Without Notice to the Attorney General, he faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison, a fine of $250,000, and three years of supervised release. He faces a maximum sentence of five years in prison, a fine of $250,000, and three years of supervised release for each conviction on the other two charges.
D’iu had his initial appearance in federal court on November 2. He is next scheduled to appear in federal court on November 24.

news.title: Meta’s Muse Charm might cost $300
news.title_en: Meta’s Muse Charm might cost $300
news.author: Jay Peters
news.article_content:
Meta is planning to price the Muse Charm, a little gadget with a screen that lets you chat with your Muse AI agent, at $300, according to The Information. CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed the gadget earlier this year and said the company expected to ship the Charm “in time for the holidays in December,” but he didn’t provide a price at the time.

When he announced the Muse Charm, Zuckerberg said that the company had “packed the whole Muse experience,” including real-time voice and avatar technology, into the gadget. It has a fingerprint sensor, and you can tap it to be able to talk to a Muse AI agent without unlocking a phone or opening an app. The Information reports that the Muse Charm will come with a free 12-month 5G data plan from Verizon.

Spokesperson Tyler Yee wrote to The Information that “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.” When reached for comment by The Verge, Yee provided the same statement.

The company is also working on a smartwatch, The Information says, but a launch for that has been pushed to 2027 as Meta tries to get Muse Charm out the door.

Meta also open sourced code to let users make their own Muse gadgets, which my colleague Sean Hollister used to make his own DIY Muse Charm.

Update, November 19th: Noted statement given by Meta spokesperson Tyler Yee.

news.title: Google is putting AI chats right on the homepage
news.title_en: Google is putting AI chats right on the homepage
news.author: Emma Roth
news.article_content:
Google is updating its homepage to include AI searches. In a post on X, Google’s vice president of product, Robby Stein, shows how you can now open a collapsible sidebar to view and continue your AI chats.

Based on the GIF shared by Stein, it looks like you can open the sidebar by clicking the gray bar that appears on the left side of your screen. From there, Google will show a list of the searches you’ve made using AI Mode, along with the ability to start a new thread, search your threads, or connect a Gemini Notebook.

It’s yet another big change for Google’s homepage, which has long presented you with a single bar to kick off your web search. The company brought its AI Mode button to its search bar last year, which opens up a chatbot-like search experience within Google. In May, Google updated its search box to accommodate longer queries and added AI-powered autocomplete.

Stein says Google is rolling out the option because “people are coming to Search with more questions that aren’t just one and done,” adding that “in testing, this sidebar made a big difference for making progress & continuing to explore the web.” The new homepage is rolling out globally on desktop.

news.title: Source: Meta plans to charge $300 for its forthcoming Muse Charm device and include a free 5G data plan from Verizon for up to 12 months (Jyoti Mann/The Information)
news.title_en: Source: Meta plans to charge $300 for its forthcoming Muse Charm device and include a free 5G data plan from Verizon for up to 12 months (Jyoti Mann/The Information)
news.author: The Information
news.article_content:
AI has an image problem, to say the least, with public fears on the rise that the technology could lead to mass unemployment and human extinction. So for its new AI agent Muse and an associated device, Meta is dialing down the fear factor and cranking up the cute. To sell AI hardware to the masses, Meta is going kawaii.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced the company's forthcoming Muse Charm on Wednesday, a handheld device for its new AI agent. It looks like a futuristic Tamagotchi and personifies the chatbot on the screen as a fuzzy, rotund beige mascot. You can name the creature yourself.

Instagram's Adam Mosseri named his "Max." (Facebook and Instagram introduced their users to the avatar this week to entice downloads of the Muse app.) "We packed the whole Muse experience, including the whole real-time voice and avatar stack, into something that fits on a keychain and is always available to talk to," Zuckerberg said at Meta Connect.

Instead of visualizing its new AI agent as non-anthropromorphic glowing orb, like Siri, or a cursor and text, like ChatGPT, Muse is a cute monster avatar. Meta could have gone down the route of its competitors, but it didn't. Instead its choice shows something about how big tech is appealing to softer emotions in the race toward mass adoption.

The Muse agent can read emails, book classes, draft documents, and make purchases (just not on Amazon, which blocked it). That cross-platform functionality means allowing Muse access to a lot of accounts, which requires trust—something Meta and social media companies at large struggle with.

If Muse and the Muse Charm are successful, however, it could prove that a mascot-led brand approach does a better job countering consumer AI fears than a disembodied voice or orb. The cuteness factor has shown up in transportation recently with vehicles like Robotaxi Zoox, Amazon delivery vans, and the DoorDash Dot delivery robot.

The vehicles are rounded in shape and designed to look non-intimidating. The trend is towards taking technology that might otherwise be seen as threatening, like autonomous vehicles or AI, and giving a friendly, charming exterior. Cuteness, research has shown, also sparks a caregiving response—quite the opposite from the feelings of fear and concern that many Americans have about AI.

While you can use Muse on a smartphone, Zuckerberg explained the Muse Charm as something you use without having to unlock a phone or open an app. It's a fun novelty that could find early adopters among people looking for a device that reduces their screentime. Zuckerberg said materials and components are being finalized for the Muse Charm and there isn't yet a price tag for the device, but the company plans to be ready to ship in time for the holidays.

news.author: Matthias Bastian
news.article_content:
US companies are using AI models more intensively than ever and paying less for the privilege.

The latest update of the Ramp AI Index, which draws on transaction data from more than 85,000 US companies, lays out the numbers. Tokens, the units of computation in which AI providers bill model usage, got 21.2 percent cheaper in six weeks, according to Ramp lead economist Ara Kharazian. At the same time, token volume rose 1.5 percent to a record high.

Token spending, meaning what companies actually pay for AI APIs, fell 6.3 percent from its peak two weeks earlier. Month over month (the week ending November 15 vs. the week ending October 18), total token spending still rose 12 percent, but token volume jumped 27.2 percent over the same span. The gap between usage and revenue keeps widening.

The average price per million tokens for OpenAI and Anthropic combined fell to $0.45, according to Ramp, down 11.2 percent from the prior month. OpenAI is cheaper at $0.38 per million tokens compared with $0.50 for Anthropic.

API routing platform OpenRouter shows a similar pattern. According to an analysis Peter Walker published on X, weekly token volume for closed-weight models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google grew 1,215 percent since the start of 2026. Weekly spending rose 455 percent over the same period, far more slowly. The spending peak came in the week of October 5, according to the OpenRouter data, which runs through the week of November 9. Spending has been declining since then.

Ramp's token metrics rely on usage and billing data imported from AI providers, while OpenRouter measures traffic through its API routing platform. The fact that both sources show a spending peak in October followed by declining outlays and rising volume reinforces the trend, though neither service is representative of the overall market. OpenRouter in particular offers only a narrow window into a very specific user base.

### Anthropic dominates the token market on IPO day

In the week ending November 15, 2026, Anthropic accounted for 58.7 percent of all token spending, according to the Ramp AI Index, up 1.7 percentage points from the prior month. Its share of token volume was even higher at 59.4 percent. OpenAI fell to 37.2 percent of spending and 37.7 percent of volume. Google came in at 1.4 percent and xAI (SpaceXAI) at 2.4 percent.

Kharazian wrote on X that Anthropic holds this share on IPO day. In October, however, Anthropic's token spending grew only 0.5 percent month over month, while OpenAI's grew 2.1 percent.
