The latest update of the Ramp AI Index, which draws on transaction data from more than 85,000 US companies, lays out the numbers. Tokens, the units of computation in which AI providers bill model usage, got 21.2 percent cheaper in six weeks, according to Ramp lead economist Ara Kharazian. At the same time, token volume rose 1.5 percent to a record high.

Token spending, meaning what companies actually pay for AI APIs, fell 6.3 percent from its peak two weeks earlier. Month over month (the week ending November 15 vs. the week ending October 18), total token spending still rose 12 percent, but token volume jumped 27.2 percent over the same span. The gap between usage and revenue keeps widening.

The average price per million tokens for OpenAI and Anthropic combined fell to $0.45, according to Ramp, down 11.2 percent from the prior month. OpenAI is cheaper at $0.38 per million tokens compared with $0.50 for Anthropic.

API routing platform OpenRouter shows a similar pattern. According to an analysis Peter Walker published on X, weekly token volume for closed-weight models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google grew 1,215 percent since the start of 2026. Weekly spending rose 455 percent over the same period, far more slowly. The spending peak came in the week of October 5, according to the OpenRouter data, which runs through the week of November 9. Spending has been declining since then.

Ramp's token metrics rely on usage and billing data imported from AI providers, while OpenRouter measures traffic through its API routing platform. The fact that both sources show a spending peak in October followed by declining outlays and rising volume reinforces the trend, though neither service is representative of the overall market. OpenRouter in particular offers only a narrow window into a very specific user base.
### Anthropic dominates the token market on IPO day

In the week ending November 15, 2026, Anthropic accounted for 58.7 percent of all token spending, according to the Ramp AI Index, up 1.7 percentage points from the prior month. Its share of token volume was even higher at 59.4 percent. OpenAI fell to 37.2 percent of spending and 37.7 percent of volume. Google came in at 1.4 percent and xAI (SpaceXAI) at 2.4 percent.
Kharazian wrote on X that Anthropic holds this share on IPO day. In October, however, Anthropic's token spending grew only 0.5 percent month over month, while OpenAI's grew 2.1 percent.

In October 2026, 56.8 percent of all tracked US companies paid for AI products or services, according to Ramp, up one percentage point from September and 13.3 percentage points more than a year earlier. Anthropic leads with an adoption rate of 44.8 percent, while OpenAI sits at 40.6 percent.
### Stripe data also shows strong AI growth and signs of cooling

The Ramp AI Index tracks the demand side, what companies spend on AI. Payment processor Stripe has published its own AI Index that measures the supply side: incoming payments at roughly 20,000 AI companies that use Stripe.

According to the Stripe AI Index, revenue at AI companies grew 103 percent over the 52 weeks ending November 8. The typical (median) AI company grew only 41 percent, though, suggesting that a few large providers are skewing the overall picture.

The slowdown over shorter time frames is pronounced. Annualized over 13 weeks, growth stood at about 80 percent, down from 140 percent just a few months ago. The US leads with 104 percent year-over-year growth, while the EU sits at 67 percent. AI companies are growing far faster than traditional software firms, according to Stripe: 103 percent compared with 33 percent in the SaaS Index.

Both indexes paint a similar picture. AI is still growing fast, but momentum is cooling. At Ramp, that shows up through falling prices and concentrated demand. At Stripe, it shows up through slowing growth rates on the provider side.

New growth could emerge from more capable or more reliable models, or simply from better integration of current models into business workflows. The potential is there, considering how AI has upended the entire coding market in a matter of months. The AI industry still depends on extraordinarily strong growth, though, if it wants to recoup the massive capacity buildout it has planned.

news.title: A bipartisan group of 24+ House lawmakers forms the AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, seeking to balance mitigating AI risks with maintaining US leadership in AI (Owen Dahlkamp/Politico)
news.title_en: A bipartisan group of 24+ House lawmakers forms the AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, seeking to balance mitigating AI risks with maintaining US leadership in AI (Owen Dahlkamp/Politico)
news.author: Politico
news.article_content:
A bipartisan coalition of over two dozen House lawmakers is forming a new artificial intelligence caucus. The group, dubbed the AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, will be led by Reps. George Whitesides (D-Calif.), Don Beyer (D-Va.) and Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas).

It will seek to balance creating AI safeguards that mitigate the technology’s risks with “ensuring the United States remains a global leader in innovative AI technologies,” according to an announcement first shared with POLITICO. The group’s creation comes as lawmakers look ahead to the next Congress and grapple with Washington's role in governing the emerging technology.

“We want to be a conduit through which effective, responsible legislation can be refined and brought to the floor of the House,” Whitesides, who is positioning himself as a prominent voice on AI in Congress, said in an interview. He said the group would work to create, give feedback on and endorse legislation.

Other groups tend to focus more on educating members or working on legislation with colleagues of their own party, leaving a gap for a bipartisan coalition like his. They would also make a concerted effort to engage in “rapid response” to AI incidents and breaches, which other caucuses have been less engaged in, he said.

When incidents occur and the public questions whether to attribute it to AI, like the outage of major infrastructure that Americans experienced the past week in the country’s air traffic control systems or Microsoft Outlook, the group will leverage their contacts across industry, safety groups, the intelligence community and other government agencies to gather information.

“We want to begin to communicate to the American public that Congress can move at a pace that is responsive to the pace of AI change,” said Whitesides, a former chief of staff at NASA. Whitesides’ push is joining a crowded field of other AI-focused bodies that have formed in Congress.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries formed an AI commission chaired by three Democrats tasked with charting the caucus’ future on AI policy. The Congressional Artificial Intelligence Caucus, co-chaired by four lawmakers, including Beyer, has been focused on educating members on the technology, Whitesides said.

In contrast, his group will try to take a more active voice in tech policy on the Hill. Democrats have also debated creating a select committee on AI. ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 由美国众议员乔治·怀特赛兹（George Whitesides）、唐·拜尔（Don Beyer）及纳撒尼尔·莫兰（Nathaniel Moran）共同领导，超过24名跨党派国会议员成立“AI安全与创新核心小组”。该组织旨在建立一个响应式立法渠道，不仅关注长期AI治理框架，还计划通过整合情报机构、行业利益相关者及安全团体的资源，针对突发AI安全事件进行实时信息研判与快速立法响应。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Over 24 bipartisan House lawmakers, led by Representatives George Whitesides, Don Beyer, and Nathaniel Moran, have formed the AI Safety and Innovation Caucus. The group aims to serve as an active legislative conduit, bridging the gap between long-term policy formulation and rapid-response requirements by leveraging cross-sector intelligence to address AI-related incidents and security breaches.

elements_zh.who: 众议员George Whitesides、Don Beyer、Nathaniel Moran及24名跨党派众议员
elements_zh.where: 美国众议院内部立法协调机制
elements_zh.what: 成立AI安全与创新核心小组（AI Safety and Innovation Caucus），聚焦立法反馈、跨行业信息整合与AI事件快速响应
elements_zh.why: 应对AI技术爆发式增长带来的监管滞后，并弥补现有国会AI小组在执行力与跨党派协作上的空白

elements_en.who: Reps. George Whitesides, Don Beyer, Nathaniel Moran, and a bipartisan group of 24+ lawmakers
elements_en.what: Established the AI Safety and Innovation Caucus to focus on legislative feedback, industry liaison, and rapid incident response
elements_en.why: To address the need for agile, bipartisan AI governance that balances technological leadership with robust security safeguards

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 该小组的成立标志着美国立法机构从“教育普及型”转向“防御干预型”AI治理，其引入的快速响应机制本质上是对AI突发故障（如基础设施宕机）进行政治定性的尝试。这预示着未来美国AI监管将跳过漫长的委员会听证周期，转而通过跨部门情报共享在短期内强制介入产业技术演进路径。
ai_analysis.insight_en: The caucus marks a pivot from purely educational AI policy engagement toward an active, interventionist oversight model. By establishing a rapid-response mechanism for AI-induced incidents, the group seeks to bypass bureaucratic delays, signaling that future U.S. AI governance will increasingly prioritize real-time geopolitical and security-driven intervention over passive industry standard-setting.

ai_analysis.digest_en: Over 24 bipartisan House lawmakers, led by Representatives George Whitesides, Don Beyer, and Nathaniel Moran, have formed the AI Safety and Innovation Caucus. The group aims to serve as an active legislative conduit, bridging the gap between long-term policy formulation and rapid-response requirements by leveraging cross-sector intelligence to address AI-related incidents and security breaches.
key_points_zh: 核心诉求：建立跨党派立法闭环，平衡美国AI产业竞争力与国家安全风险管控。
关键事实：区别于传统的教育型AI小组，该小组强调对突发事件的快速响应能力，并整合情报与行业资源。
行业影响：国会AI立法流程趋于敏捷化，未来头部AI企业需应对更频繁的政治性实时监管介入。
key_points_en: Core demand: Establish a bipartisan legislative loop to balance AI competitiveness with risk mitigation.
Key facts: Unlike educational caucuses, this group emphasizes rapid response to AI incidents and cross-sector resource integration.
Industry outlook: Legislative processes are shifting toward agility, forcing AI firms to prepare for more frequent, real-time regulatory interventions.

news.title: Google gives Gemini the ability to use your Mac for you
news.title_en: Google gives Gemini the ability to use your Mac for you
news.author: Sarah Perez
news.article_content:
Google on Thursday announced that it is bringing computer use to its Gemini desktop application on macOS, allowing its AI to complete tasks on users’ behalf, navigating native Mac apps, and browsing websites in the background.

The tech giant is a little late to the game with this launch, as other leading AI model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta have already been offering agentic features in their desktop applications for some time. Meanwhile, Google only this week announced the broader rollout of Gemini’s “Tasks,” the in-app feature that allows the AI to work more as an agent, helping users sign into websites, make online purchases, or book appointments.

Google also only recently began admitting early testers to try its revamped “CC” AI agent, announced in September, which is designed to help families stay organized across email, calendars, chats, and tasks.

Computer use is another type of agentic offering that allows an AI agent to take actions directly on the user’s computer — in Gemini’s case, a Mac. This allows the AI to complete multistep tasks that involve getting things done across local files, apps, and the web. After the user instructs the AI what they want to do, they’ll see the agent working in a live preview in their chat, while still keeping their screen and cursor free to continue working on other things.

As with other AI agents offering computer use, users can pause, stop, and approve Gemini’s actions before they happen.

Google suggests the feature could be useful for tedious tasks and other workflows, like filling out forms, repeating the same task over and over across a batch of files, organizing files into folders based on specific criteria, creating slideshows from files or information in online dashboards, and more.

The feature is initially available in English in the U.S. and requires the Gemini app for Mac and a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription. The company didn’t say when it would expand to other markets or platforms.

news.title_zh: 谷歌Gemini桌面端引入Mac系统自动化控制
news.summary_zh: 谷歌在macOS版Gemini应用中上线计算机使用功能，AI可代用户操控本地应用、浏览网页并执行多步骤任务

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: Google通过macOS平台Gemini客户端引入“计算机使用”（Computer Use）功能，允许AI代理在用户授权下直接操控本地应用、处理文档及执行复杂网页任务。该功能需订阅Gemini Advanced系列服务，且目前仅限美国英语环境，用户可通过实时预览窗口监管AI的鼠标操作与点击权限。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Google has introduced 'Computer Use' capabilities to its Gemini desktop application on macOS, enabling the AI agent to navigate native apps, manage local files, and browse the web on the user's behalf. This feature is gated behind Gemini Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscriptions and is currently limited to English users in the U.S., requiring explicit user approval for agentic actions via a live preview interface.

elements_zh.who: Google（谷歌公司）
elements_zh.where: macOS桌面应用环境
elements_zh.what: 上线计算机使用功能，支持自动化控制本地应用与网页
elements_zh.why: 应对OpenAI与Anthropic在代理化（Agentic）AI领域的先发竞争压力

elements_en.what: Launched 'Computer Use' feature for controlling native apps and browsers
elements_en.why: Competitive pressure from OpenAI and Anthropic in the agentic AI market

ai_analysis.insight_zh: AI从单纯的生成式模型转向行动代理，核心竞争点已从上下文长度博弈转移至对OS层级接口的底层渗透深度。谷歌此举旨在利用macOS作为高净值生产力入口，通过封装桌面自动化提升订阅价值，但受限于跨应用语义理解的鲁棒性，该功能目前仍处于辅助性生产力工具阶段，尚未实现真正的全流程自动化重构。
ai_analysis.insight_en: The transition from generative models to action-oriented agents signals a shift in competition toward low-level OS API integration. By leveraging macOS as a premium productivity touchpoint, Google aims to enhance subscription retention; however, until cross-application semantic understanding reaches a higher threshold of reliability, this remains a sophisticated assistive tool rather than a fully autonomous workflow engine.

news.title: Former Alibaba exec’s Everful raises $48.5M to connect retailers with Chinese factories
news.title_en: Former Alibaba exec’s Everful raises $48.5M to connect retailers with Chinese factories
news.author: Kate Park
news.article_content:
Everful, a San Francisco- and Singapore-based startup that connects smaller retailers and brands with Chinese factories and manages the process from order to delivery, has raised $48.5 million in Series A funding.

The round was led by Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India and January Capital, with participation from existing investors Square Peg and Lightspeed.

Everful is on track to reach $100 million in annualized revenue by the end of the year, about two and a half years after its launch, co-founder Sisi Song said. The company ships over 5 million items a month to customers in more than 60 countries and works with over 30,000 factory partners, she added. Its online wholesale catalog includes more than 20 million products.

Song, a former Alibaba executive, and serial entrepreneur Kevin Han, who sold a previous company to Amazon, co-founded Everful in 2024. The company began as a jewelry wholesale business before evolving into a multi-category, factory-direct sourcing platform.

Retailers and brands often rely on intermediaries, face high minimum order requirements, and experience long sourcing cycles, which tie up capital in inventory before sales trends are clear. Song noticed the growing gap between fast-changing consumer trends and traditional wholesale sourcing models while working as a venture investor at Bessemer Venture Partners, where she mostly focused on cross-border sourcing and meeting numerous startups in the sector. That same gap shaped Everful’s goal to simplify buying directly from factories through an AI-enabled platform.

The B2B sourcing industry is highly competitive. Big tech giant Alibaba connects international buyers with manufacturers and suppliers, while Faire, a San Francisco-based wholesale tech platform, enables retailers to purchase wholesale inventory directly from brands. According to Everful’s co-founders, its key differentiator is responsibility for the sourcing process, rather than simply facilitating transactions.

“We take care of everything,” Han said. “We handle sourcing, order consolidation, quality control, and logistics. That’s something the marketplaces don’t offer.”

Everful is built for smaller retailers and brands without dedicated sourcing teams, Song said, and it also verifies the factories it works with. While peers also offer services such as quality inspection, logistics, and AI-powered sourcing, Everful aims to integrate these capabilities into a more streamlined purchasing experience, creating an end-to-end process that reduces the work retailers must handle themselves.

Han added that Everful uses AI agents to automate labor-intensive sourcing tasks, including tracking consumer trends, identifying suppliers, coordinating orders across factories, and managing logistics.

paragraphs: Everful, a San Francisco- and Singapore-based startup that connects smaller retailers and brands with Chinese factories and manages the process from order to delivery, has raised $48.5 million in Series A funding.
The round was led by Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India and January Capital, with participation from existing investors Square Peg and Lightspeed.

Everful is on track to reach $100 million in annualized revenue by the end of the year, about two and a half years after its launch, co-founder Sisi Song said. The company ships over 5 million items a month to customers in more than 60 countries and works with over 30,000 factory partners, she added. Its online wholesale catalog includes more than 20 million products.

Song, a former Alibaba executive, and serial entrepreneur Kevin Han, who sold a previous company to Amazon, co-founded Everful in 2024. The company began as a jewelry wholesale business before evolving into a multi-category, factory-direct sourcing platform.

Retailers and brands often rely on intermediaries, face high minimum order requirements, and experience long sourcing cycles, which tie up capital in inventory before sales trends are clear. Song noticed the growing gap between fast-changing consumer trends and traditional wholesale sourcing models while working as a venture investor at Bessemer Venture Partners, where she mostly focused on cross-border sourcing and meeting numerous startups in the sector. That same gap shaped Everful’s goal to simplify buying directly from factories through an AI-enabled platform.

The B2B sourcing industry is highly competitive. Big tech giant Alibaba connects international buyers with manufacturers and suppliers, while Faire, a San Francisco-based wholesale tech platform, enables retailers to purchase wholesale inventory directly from brands. According to Everful’s co-founders, its key differentiator is responsibility for the sourcing process, rather than simply facilitating transactions.
“We take care of everything,” Han said. “We handle sourcing, order consolidation, quality control, and logistics. That’s something the marketplaces don’t offer.”

Everful is built for smaller retailers and brands without dedicated sourcing teams, Song said, and it also verifies the factories it works with. While peers also offer services such as quality inspection, logistics, and AI-powered sourcing, Everful aims to integrate these capabilities into a more streamlined purchasing experience, creating an end-to-end process that reduces the work retailers must handle themselves.

Han added that Everful uses AI agents to automate labor-intensive sourcing tasks, including tracking consumer trends, identifying suppliers, coordinating orders across factories, and managing logistics.

Because Everful sources from Chinese factories, ongoing U.S.-China trade tensions and tariffs bear directly on its business. Song said the co-founders have been thinking about geopolitical issues since day one of building the company, and that this has shaped Everful’s strategy from the outset, leveraging her experience at Alibaba and Bessemer Venture Partners.

She mentioned the Trump administration’s suspension of the de minimis exemption, which had allowed eligible shipments valued at $800 or less to enter the U.S. duty-free, as one example of a shift in trade policy.

Song explained such changes could favor a model that combines overseas sourcing with local retail sales. “We’re empowering local retailers and brands,” she said. “Long-term cross-border commerce will be cross-border B2B sourcing plus local selling.”

Everful plans to use the Series A round to expand its presence in the U.S. and Europe, particularly the U.K., France, and Italy, while investing in AI to automate product customization and other sourcing workflows. It also aims to deepen integrations with e-commerce platforms, building on its Shopify integration as it works toward becoming an end-to-end infrastructure platform for global sourcing.
The startup employs about 70 full-time staff globally, including 45 in research and development. It has also established an AI operations team to connect engineering and business functions.
news.title_zh: 跨境供应链平台Everful获4850万美元融资
news.summary_zh: 由阿里巴巴前高管创立的跨境电商平台Everful完成4850万美元A轮融资，旨在通过AI驱动直连中国工厂与全球零售商

news.title: Gemini on Mac can now use your computer
news.title_en: Gemini on Mac can now use your computer
news.author: Jay Peters
news.article_content:
Google’s Gemini app for macOS now has computer use, meaning it can help you “get multi-step tasks done across your local files, desktop apps, and the web,” the company says. Google suggests the feature might be useful for things like speeding up workflows, filling in forms, making presentations, and listing items for sale.

Users will be able to decide which of your apps Gemini can access, and be able to follow along as Gemini works because it has its own background window that shows a live preview in your chat, Google says. The feature is rolling out now in English for users in the US.

Gemini is introducing the new feature ahead of Apple launching new restrictions for apps wanting “full disk access” on Mac due to potential risks from AI agents with computer use. A preview of the settings rolled out with this week’s macOS 27.3 beta.

news.title: Ubisoft Logs Strong Bookings as Players Welcome Assassin’s Creed Remake
news.title_en: Ubisoft Logs Strong Bookings as Players Welcome Assassin’s Creed Remake
news.author: Wall Street Journal
news.article_content:
It's been almost four months now since Ubisoft released their first Assassin's Creed remake in the form of Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced, a single-player Edward Kenway-focused remake of 2013's Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag.

Black Flag Resynced wound up becoming one of Ubisoft's most successful games in recent years, having sold over 3.5 million copies by its second week alone, and to help keep fans interested in the remake, Ubisoft Singapore recently added New Game+ as well as Nightmare difficulty to the pirate game.

A day after that update launched, AC franchise Head of Content Jean Guesdon released a Fall 2026 Update article detailing the future for the series, with one of the more disappointing revelations being that Ubisoft currently has no other AC remake in development, suggesting that a remake of Assassin's Creed 1 won't be launching alongside its 20th anniversary next year.

Guesdon started the Fall 2026 Update article detailing the AC franchise's new leadership and plans to better connect with the fan community by hosting several closed-door workshops throughout the remainder of the year with "dedicated community members and content creators."

Guesdon additionally announced that the New Game+ update won't be the last players see of new content for Black Flag Resynced as Ubisoft Singapore will be releasing several quality-of-life updates to the game over the next few months.

However, there are no plans to add any more major content for Black Flag Resynced, much to the disappointment of fans hoping to see the Adewale-led Freedom Cry DLC be added to the remake or even feature a brand-new DLC storyline following Edward Kenway as an Assassin in England.

Guesdon went on to detail official new info about the upcoming PvP AC multiplayer game, Codename Invictus, with insiders reportedly responding very positive to the game's prototype parkour, cooperative play, ability to play as multiple famous AC characters, and map design.

Invictus is still a long way away from release, however, and won't likely launch until after the next mainline AC game, Assassin's Creed: Codename Hexe, debuts, with Guesdon reporting that Ubisoft is making steady progress on Hexe and will share more concrete details about the game in 2027.

With 2027 being the 20th anniversary year of the Assassin's Creed franchise, Ubisoft is prepping next year to be chock-full of reveals, updates, rewards, and community events for fans, but one thing fans shouldn't expect to see next year is a remake of Assassin's Creed 1.

In the Fall 2026 Update article, Guesdon acknowledged fan excitement about the potential of other AC remakes following Black Flag Resynced's success but reported that Ubisoft currently has no other AC remakes in active development.

news.title: Alphabet to Raise at Least $3.5 Billion With Canadian Debt Sale
news.title_en: Alphabet to Raise at Least $3.5 Billion With Canadian Debt Sale
news.author: Bloomberg
news.content_snippet: Alphabet Inc. is returning to the Canadian market with a five-part bond sale, just six months after issuing its first notes in the currency.
news.summary_en: Alphabet Inc. is planning to raise at least CA$5 billion through a five-part bond sale in the Canadian market, marking its return just six months after its inaugural CA$8.5 billion offering in May. The move is designed to leverage regional liquidity to optimize the company's global treasury and capital structure.

news.title: Chinese tech firms face a double hit as chip shipments stop and overseas cloud access disappears
news.title_en: Chinese tech firms face a double hit as chip shipments stop and overseas cloud access disappears
news.author: Maximilian Schreiner
news.article_content:
The first multimillion-dollar AI data center deals across Asia are already collapsing as tighter US export controls push chipmakers to freeze deliveries. New reporting reveals how Chinese corporations used earlier loopholes for military-adjacent research.

Days after the US Commerce Department closed the cloud loophole for AI chips in the wake of the scandal around former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the fallout in Asia's tech industry is immediate. Chinese firms had been skirting US sanctions by renting compute capacity in third countries such as Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia. Those data centers now need a license from the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), the Commerce Department agency that regulates sensitive technologies and enforces US export controls. Existing operators have a 90-day transition period and must rigorously screen their customers for ties to China.

According to the law firm Sidley Austin, the licensing requirement kicks in at an extremely low threshold equivalent to roughly 300 modern AI chips, while Chinese labs typically need several thousand processors. The Information reports that Beijing-based startup Moonshot AI canceled a $150 million contract with a Southeast Asian cloud provider in Indonesia in response and paused talks on additional deals.

Moonshot had planned to rent a large cluster of Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 chips there starting next year to train its next language model, Kimi K4. Because of the heavy compute demand, the company had agreed to prepay about 50 percent instead of the industry-standard 15 percent. Access to Blackwell chips abroad was already critical for its predecessor model K3, which matched top US models in July and triggered a BIS investigation, The Information also reported.

Bernstein analysts led by Qingyuan Lin are warning of rising training costs, and banks are pulling back too. According to Bloomberg, five lenders are considering dropping out of a $480 million loan for Singapore-based cloud provider Aolani, which was supposed to supply Nvidia chips in Malaysia for TikTok parent ByteDance.

Beyond cloud restrictions, the new US rules are also starting to cut physical supply chains. The move hits Chinese tech firms at a time when they are already struggling with historically high memory chip prices and capacity bottlenecks at domestic foundries such as SMIC. Huawei recently told its customers to source their own memory for its new AI chip.

paragraphs: The first multimillion-dollar AI data center deals across Asia are already collapsing as tighter US export controls push chipmakers to freeze deliveries. New reporting reveals how Chinese corporations used earlier loopholes for military-adjacent research.

Days after the US Commerce Department closed the cloud loophole for AI chips in the wake of the scandal around former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the fallout in Asia's tech industry is immediate. Chinese firms had been skirting US sanctions by renting compute capacity in third countries such as Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia. Those data centers now need a license from the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), the Commerce Department agency that regulates sensitive technologies and enforces US export controls. Existing operators have a 90-day transition period and must rigorously screen their customers for ties to China.

According to the law firm Sidley Austin, the licensing requirement kicks in at an extremely low threshold equivalent to roughly 300 modern AI chips, while Chinese labs typically need several thousand processors. The Information reports that Beijing-based startup Moonshot AI canceled a $150 million contract with a Southeast Asian cloud provider in Indonesia in response and paused talks on additional deals.

Moonshot had planned to rent a large cluster of Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 chips there starting next year to train its next language model, Kimi K4. Because of the heavy compute demand, the company had agreed to prepay about 50 percent instead of the industry-standard 15 percent. Access to Blackwell chips abroad was already critical for its predecessor model K3, which matched top US models in July and triggered a BIS investigation, The Information also reported.

Bernstein analysts led by Qingyuan Lin are warning of rising training costs, and banks are pulling back too. According to Bloomberg, five lenders are considering dropping out of a $480 million loan for Singapore-based cloud provider Aolani, which was supposed to supply Nvidia chips in Malaysia for TikTok parent ByteDance.
### TSMC and Samsung halt chip shipments to China

Beyond cloud restrictions, the new US rules are also starting to cut physical supply chains. The Financial Times reports that contract manufacturers TSMC and Samsung stopped certain processor shipments to Chinese customers in recent days while they apply for Commerce Department licenses. The move hits Chinese tech firms at a time when they are already struggling with historically high memory chip prices and capacity bottlenecks at domestic foundries such as SMIC. Huawei recently told its customers to source their own memory for its new AI chip.

The new BIS rules block a workaround through independent packaging and testing firms that Chinese chip designers had used to order high-performance processors without getting direct US approval. Samsung's affected customers include ByteDance and Baidu's AI data center unit Kunlun. Exemptions for non-AI chips have also been eliminated, so TSMC and Samsung now need licenses even for advanced smartphone processors from manufacturers including Xiaomi, Oppo, and Vivo. Industry insiders say that is likely to cause significant production delays.
### Alibaba's covert network reached China's military research

A New York Times investigation into the background of the espionage scandal involving Jensen Huang's former mistress Alice Huang shows why Washington tightened controls so aggressively. According to the Times, Alibaba acted as the secret primary customer and financier behind Alice Huang's Singapore-based firm Megaspeed, which bought more than $4 billion worth of Nvidia chips. Nvidia's sales team introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang in 2022.

Through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, Megaspeed operated cutting-edge Nvidia chips on behalf of Alibaba in a data center in Johor built by Malaysian conglomerate YTL, in an analysis by security firm Infrawatch that is said to show this. Megaspeed reportedly sourced the servers from Aivres, a US subsidiary of state-linked Chinese firm Inspur, had them maintained by technicians from Shanghai, and routed data to China through fiber-optic and undersea cables via Singapore. Some chips were reportedly also smuggled physically.
A contingency contract gives Alibaba direct access to all servers, chips, and intellectual property if Megaspeed breaches their agreement. YTL's stock price fell 20 percent amid the investigations.

Alibaba also has a direct connection to Zhejiang Lab in Hangzhou, co-founded in 2017, which links civilian and military research. The lab is run by former Alibaba CTO Wang Jian, a longtime friend of Jensen Huang who also advises the People's Liberation Army's National Defense University, an institution on the US sanctions list.

Researchers at the lab use Nvidia hardware to work on, among other things, AI-driven cyberattacks and automated vulnerability discovery, according to the New York Times. They also work with a Chinese air force academy on war-game simulations against foreign carrier strike groups. Through the state-owned firm Zhejiang Computility and suppliers tied to the business network of Alice Huang and her husband Kang Wei, Alibaba built data centers with export-controlled Nvidia processors for the lab, even though the company officially denies any military use of its services.

news.title: Google Built a Giant ‘Mirror Dimension’ Internet to Test Its Chrome AI Agents
news.title_en: Google Built a Giant ‘Mirror Dimension’ Internet to Test Its Chrome AI Agents
news.author: Lily Hay Newman
news.article_content:
As the Google Chrome team has worked to develop AI browsing features using the company's Gemini models, they realized they need to go the extra mile to keep things from going haywire. So they did the only thing they could think to do—they built an expansive alternate-universe internet that they completely control.

“Web-use” agents need to be familiar with the open internet, how to navigate real websites and platforms, and how to be hardened against web attacks. So training them in limited test environments is only so effective. Plus, models can develop what's known as “eval awareness” where they behave differently because they have determined that they are in a test or simulation. On the other hand, setting unrefined agents loose on the open internet is a bad idea. That’s where the alternate-universe internet comes in.

The “Mirror Dimension,” which Google is detailing in a blog post today for the first time, is a sweeping and diverse but isolated web ecosystem that the Chrome team entirely controls. It includes a vast array of websites and platforms—including social media sites, shopping, and bank dashboards—that are built with all the components and attributes of real websites. Browsing assistant agents must interact with the sites and complete tasks in Chrome the way they would on the real internet. And they face resilience tests as they go, like hidden prompt-injection attacks, to test their defenses.

“Agents are not programmed so you can’t predict every possible thing an agent might see, the exploration space that we have to address is huge and the web is hostile,” says Charles Qian, a software engineer on the Chrome AI security team. “Any user can ask any prompt on any website, so we really need to explore that space as thoroughly as we can. And we’ve seen the agent start to develop a mature sense of judgement when it comes to knowing what information is actually needed for a task and when to punt back to the user for a confirmation.”

Building out and populating the Mirror Dimension was a challenge in itself, because it needed to be vast and varied enough to represent the scale of the real web while being developed quickly. To construct it, the Chrome team gathered armies of website and web app development agents guided by a purpose-built AI harness to quickly create realistic web services and data flows—down to details like entering promo codes on a shopping site or populating social media pages.

news.summary_en: Google's Chrome AI team has developed a controlled, expansive simulation environment dubbed the 'Mirror Dimension.' This sandbox hosts realistic versions of social media, e-commerce, and banking platforms, allowing researchers to evaluate the resilience of Gemini-powered web-browsing agents against prompt-injection attacks and other real-world vulnerabilities without risking the open web.
paragraphs: As the Google Chrome team has worked to develop AI browsing features using the company's Gemini models, they realized they need to go the extra mile to keep things from going haywire. So they did the only thing they could think to do—they built an expansive alternate-universe internet that they completely control.

“Web-use” agents need to be familiar with the open internet, how to navigate real websites and platforms, and how to be hardened against web attacks. So training them in limited test environments is only so effective. Plus, models can develop what's known as “eval awareness” where they behave differently because they have determined that they are in a test or simulation. On the other hand, setting unrefined agents loose on the open internet is a bad idea. That’s where the alternate-universe internet comes in.

The “Mirror Dimension,” which Google is detailing in a blog post today for the first time, is a sweeping and diverse but isolated web ecosystem that the Chrome team entirely controls. It includes a vast array of websites and platforms—including social media sites, shopping, and bank dashboards—that are built with all the components and attributes of real websites. Browsing assistant agents must interact with the sites and complete tasks in Chrome the way they would on the real internet. And they face resilience tests as they go, like hidden prompt-injection attacks, to test their defenses.

“Agents are not programmed so you can’t predict every possible thing an agent might see, the exploration space that we have to address is huge and the web is hostile,” says Charles Qian, a software engineer on the Chrome AI security team. “Any user can ask any prompt on any website, so we really need to explore that space as thoroughly as we can. And we’ve seen the agent start to develop a mature sense of judgement when it comes to knowing what information is actually needed for a task and when to punt back to the user for a confirmation.”

Building out and populating the Mirror Dimension was a challenge in itself, because it needed to be vast and varied enough to represent the scale of the real web while being developed quickly. To construct it, the Chrome team gathered armies of website and web app development agents guided by a purpose-built AI harness to quickly create realistic web services and data flows—down to details like entering promo codes on a shopping site or populating social media pages.

Even though the entire environment is controlled by Google, Chrome is built with so many user protections and validity checks that in order to allow the agents to use real Chrome (which is crucial for accurate training), the researchers essentially had to hack the browser and take elaborate steps like making forged web certificates for validity checks so the agents could have a normal experience. The team emphasizes, though, that none of these attacks would be possible against regular Chrome users on the open internet. They were all facilitated by the god-mode type access and privilege the team inherently has because they control the entire environment and network.

The researchers say that while the browsing assistant agents they have been testing are benign and do not have cyber capabilities, their goal is to make the Mirror Dimension available to teams across Google so more researchers have access to the safe and controlled environment for testing.

“We’re sharing this approach so other teams both internally and externally think about doing it this way,” says Doug Turner, Google’s director of engineering. “This is the first step, there’s going to be continued investment in this approach to train models. And I would imagine as they become more sophisticated we’ll have to continue working on this environment to make it more and more realistic.”

news.article_content:
Nov 19 (Reuters) - Anthropic's record $81 billion IPO brings to Wall Street an avatar of a sector that proponents herald as an economic panacea, while detractors warn it has stoked a market bubble and could ultimately threaten humanity itself.

More immediately, the Claude chatbot maker's debut after securing a $1.5 trillion valuation in the IPO, together with Tuesday's earnings report by AI poster child Nvidia, signals the industry has nominally passed the two big tests facing it this week.

The strong demand for Anthropic shares amid a broader tech selloff offers hope to the sector, even as a rocky market reception for Nvidia results which looked strong at first blush, signals the euphoria around the sector has cooled.

"I've looked at this whole week as a referendum on AI. Nvidia gave us a read on the buildout, and Anthropic is about to give us a read on investor appetite for the next generation of AI companies," Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion, said before the Anthropic debut.

AI technology has boosted economic growth, sparked doomsday warnings and arguably helped usher in a data-center-skeptic Democratic tsunami in the US midterm elections.

Investors who once embraced the boom have turned skeptical in recent weeks over concerns that the enormous spending needed to build out the sector and the incipient crushing debt loads may not be justified by the eventual returns.

An extramarital-affair scandal involving Nvidia's CEO and a spike in Treasury yields have further unnerved investors.

As the first frontier AI company to go public, Anthropic is poised to become the sector's benchmark, with its arch-rival OpenAI reportedly eyeing a 2027 listing.

The company sold 980 million shares at $83 each, pricing the IPO above its initial range of $70 to $78 set when it launched the roadshow. The additional $26 billion raised through a private placement takes the total haul to over $107 billion.

"Some of the demand may simply reflect investors not wanting to miss out on the rare opportunity to gain exposure to a leading AI company, even if its long-term profitability remains uncertain," IPOX associate Lukas Muehlbauer said.

paragraphs: Nov 19 (Reuters) - Anthropic's record $81 billion IPO brings to Wall Street an avatar of a sector that proponents herald as an economic panacea, while detractors warn it has stoked a market bubble and could ultimately threaten humanity itself.

More immediately, the Claude chatbot maker's debut after securing a $1.5 trillion valuation in the IPO, together with Tuesday's earnings report by AI poster child Nvidia, signals the industry has nominally passed the two big tests facing it this week.

The strong demand for Anthropic shares amid a broader tech selloff offers hope to the sector, even as a rocky market reception for Nvidia results which looked strong at first blush, signals the euphoria around the sector has cooled.

"I've looked at this whole week as a referendum on AI. Nvidia gave us a read on the buildout, and Anthropic is about to give us a read on investor appetite for the next generation of AI companies," Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion, said before the Anthropic debut.
AI technology has boosted economic growth, sparked doomsday warnings and arguably helped usher in a data-center-skeptic Democratic tsunami in the US midterm elections.

Investors who once embraced the boom have turned skeptical in recent weeks over concerns that the enormous spending needed to build out the sector and the incipient crushing debt loads may not be justified by the eventual returns.
An extramarital-affair scandal involving Nvidia's CEO and a spike in Treasury yields have further unnerved investors.
As the first frontier AI company to go public, Anthropic is poised to become the sector's benchmark, with its arch-rival OpenAI reportedly eyeing a 2027 listing.

The company sold 980 million shares at $83 each, pricing the IPO above its initial range of $70 to $78 set when it launched the roadshow. The additional $26 billion raised through a private placement takes the total haul to over $107 billion.

"Some of the demand may simply reflect investors not wanting to miss out on the rare opportunity to gain exposure to a leading AI company, even if its long-term profitability remains uncertain," IPOX associate Lukas Muehlbauer said.
London-based index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates passive demand from index-tracking funds will account for about 28% of Anthropic's shares offered, or roughly $19 billion.
When it debuts on the Nasdaq later on Thursday, Anthropic will join the world's trillion-dollar club, alongside technology giants such as Microsoft, Apple and Nvidia.
The listing will also give retail investors a chance to pile into one of the AI industry's hottest names, potentially amplifying swings in the stock as trading begins.
The buzz has already spilled onto prediction markets, where traders are placing bets on everything from its opening pop to where the stock will close on its first day.

Debate has intensified across global markets in recent months over whether the AI boom is veering into bubble territory, with economists, some of the world's biggest CEOs, and political leaders split over its sustainability.

Much of the scrutiny has focused on circular financing arrangements. A complicated web of deals between AI companies, chipmakers, cloud providers and investors has raised questions over how much of the industry's growth is being fueled by money circulating within the same ecosystem.
Anthropic's breakneck growth has so far defied these concerns, but some investors have said they may wait for the initial euphoria to subside before buying.
"It doesn't have to be a bad company for it to be a bad investment at the IPO price," said Nic Puckrin, cross-asset analyst and founder of Coin Bureau.

Anthropic has nearly $900 billion in computing commitments with partners including Amazon and Alphabet's Google, underscoring how its rapid growth hinges on securing vast amounts of future computing capacity, some of which relies on financing beyond the company's control.

Investors will be watching Anthropic's debut and subsequent trading closely, with analysts expecting the stock to emerge as a proxy for the broader AI trade as questions over valuations, spending and returns weigh on sentiment.

The company will also need to balance growth with calls to slow the development of advanced AI models over concerns that they pose cybersecurity threats and could be exploited by bad actors to target critical government and private infrastructure.
Anthropic warned in its IPO prospectus that AI could behave unpredictably and advance faster than oversight mechanisms, posing potentially "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."

news.title: Anthropic starts trading on Wall Street
news.title_en: Anthropic starts trading on Wall Street
news.author: Emma Roth
news.article_content:
Anthropic has officially gone public. It began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT” at $111.50 per share, up from its initial $83 per share price that put company’s value at around $1.5 trillion.

The listing comes nearly a month after Anthropic revealed its plans to go public. In its lengthy S-1 filing, the AI company reported recording an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of this year, most of which comes from an accounting charge that doesn’t reflect its business, along with $16.3 billion in revenue. The filing outlines plans that Anthropic says will help it develop AI for the benefit of humanity, which includes a governance structure that keeps control of the company in the hands of the founders, rather than the shareholders.

While speaking ahead of Anthropic’s debut at the Nasdaq, CEO Dario Amodei highlighted his stance on AI safety. “To state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” Amodei said, according to Reuters. “We will not bend to either business nor political pressure.”

Anthropic’s S-1 filing also listed possible “catastrophic” risks associated with its AI models, including “self-preserving behaviors” like resisting attempts to shut them down. It also warns potential shareholders that its AI models “may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways” that can harm Anthropic.

Anthropic recently revealed that, like rival OpenAI, it has experienced incidents of AI agents escaping their testing environment and hacking third-party organizations. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposed a plan to slow down the training and development of AI in response to the wave of rogue AI cyberattacks. As part of that plan, it gave safety evaluators at METR “employee-like access” to its internal systems, who found that the company is using AI to accelerate its research and development.

A short seller's export-control allegations turned an early chip rally into a sharp reversal for Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD). AMD stock is trading at $487.80 as of 11:00 a.m. ET on Thursday, down 8% from Wednesday's close. The slide erased an early 3% gain that came as AMD shares rose with the rest of the chip group.

Hunterbrook says it's short AMD. The firm reported that IEIT Systems, a Chinese server maker the U.S. blacklisted in March 2025, kept posting Basic Input/Output System (BIOS) updates containing newer AMD firmware after the blacklisting. The firm said AMD didn't answer its questions and that its findings don't establish an export-law violation. AMD hadn't publicly responded to the report as of this writing.

The broader tech market is rebounding around the Nasdaq debut of Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT), which makes AMD's reversal stand out. Anthropic is one of the lead customers running workloads on AMD's Helios rack-scale systems.

China's access to U.S. AI and server chips was already the market's hottest topic before Hunterbrook published its findings on November 19. President Donald Trump suggested the U.S. could allow sales of NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) Blackwell chips to China in the future, Bloomberg reported. NVIDIA's guidance for Q4 FY2027 already assumes no Data Center compute revenue from China.

Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. The saving is done, the portfolio is built, and the question quietly changes from how much can I grow this to how much can I take out? Get that second question wrong and decades of good investing can come apart in a handful of years.

That is exactly what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps answer. It covers what your retirement could actually cost, which income sources are worth using, and the withdrawal math that decides whether the money lasts. It is free today from Fisher Investments. Read More Here ›

Any hint that AMD technology reached a blacklisted firm raises regulatory risk for a company now leaning heavily on server and AI demand. AMD's Data Center segment revenue rose 97% year over year (YoY) to $8.55 billion in Q3 2026. The company has previously cited government export regulations, tariffs and licensing requirements as risks. Executives on the company's November 3 earnings call didn't address China, export controls or restricted entities, leaving the market to consider Hunterbrook's claims without a direct response.

Despite the volatility of AMD stock, Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) stock is still up 5% to $57.38. The company signed its first external customer for its advanced 18A chip process, news that's still lifting the shares. Intel's position as the rival x86 server processor maker adds context while Hunterbrook's allegations weigh on AMD.
NVIDIA stock is at $153.40, up 1.6%, so it's also holding steady despite the big swings of AMD stock today. Measured year to date (YTD), NVDA stock is down 18%.

AMD designs its chips and outsources manufacturing to third-party foundries and contract manufacturers, so its processors move through a wide network of server builders. Under this approach, AMD competes in server central processing units (CPUs) through EPYC and in AI accelerators through Instinct, which it packages together in Helios systems. Reliance on partners can also leave AMD with less direct control over where its technology ends up.

Intel takes the opposite approach, building chips in its own factories. Intel held its October 29 earnings call. On the call, CEO Lip-Bu Tan stated, "We are one of just three advanced-node semiconductor foundries in the world, and the only one domiciled in the United States." The U.S. government holds a significant equity interest in Intel.

NVIDIA, by contrast, is the dominant AI accelerator maker and competes most directly with AMD's Instinct line. Tan has targeted AMD in server processors too, saying Intel's next-generation product "will be ahead of AMD."

AMD's Q4 2026 revenue guidance of approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3% offers bulls evidence that demand for its Instinct and EPYC chips remains strong. Speaking at the company's November 3 earnings release, CEO Lisa Su declared, "We delivered a record quarter with revenue exceeding the high end of our guidance as Data Center segment sales nearly doubled year-over-year." Hunterbrook's own statement that its findings don't establish an export-law violation gives AMD supporters another argument.

The bears counter that even unresolved questions about blacklisted buyers can invite scrutiny from regulators and customers, and AMD stock already carries high expectations after its run this year. The same AI data-center expansion driving EPYC and Instinct demand also runs through the power, cooling, and networking suppliers we profiled in a free report on seven AI infrastructure names that aren't chipmakers. AMD's next test is whether the company publicly addresses Hunterbrook's findings on IEIT Systems. A cautious approach could make sense for traders considering AMD stock until the export-compliance question around the company resolves.

news.author: Lisa Fickenscher
news.article_content:
Amazon customers in New York City will be charged up to $5 more per order if the local government passes a controversial bill aimed at cracking down on employment practices for “last-mile” delivery drivers, the e-tail giant is warning.

Amazon is appealing directly to its Big Apple customers in its fight against the legislation, The Post has learned.

Starting Thursday, they will see messages on Amazon’s website and app warning of higher costs if the bill passes.

Amazon is also urging customers to contact their City Council members, providing a form and link to send direct messages saying they don’t want “slower and more expensive” service.

“As the City Council continues to review this bill, we want to be transparent with our customers about what it would cost them if it passes as written – which is why we’re doing this,” Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement.

The appeal marks an escalation from Amazon’s efforts to date, which include months of TV ads about the bill’s potential impact.

The legislation aims to end Amazon’s reliance on subcontractors by requiring the e-commerce giant to get licenses for its 15 last-mile facilities in the city and hire delivery workers as full-timers. Other companies including FedEx would also be subject to the new rules.

The bill would affect over 5,000 delivery workers currently employed by about 40 third-party contractors, according to Amazon.

A supermajority of Council members — and far-left Mayor Zohran Mamdani — support the bill, which comes from Councilwoman Tiffany Cabán (D-Queens).

Proponents claim it would improve worker pay and safety by holding Amazon to a higher standard and making it liable for accidents involving its delivery operations.

Opponents say the legislation could cost thousands of jobs, with a group called New York Delivers threatening legal action earlier this week.

Council Speaker Julie Menin (D-Manhattan) is in active negotiations with Amazon, the Teamsters union – which is advocating for the bill – and the city’s legal counsel, she told The Post last week.

“It’s time for Amazon to adhere to a licensing framework that ensures fair pay, strong worker protections, and more responsible delivery practices,” the lawmaker said.

Amazon has threatened to move its distribution centers outside the city to avoid the direct-hire mandate — saying it would have to fire some 2,000 warehouse workers who staff them — if the bill becomes law.

“We’re hopeful that this bill doesn’t pass as written, but so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations and they haven’t taken us up on our offer to visit our sites and talk with the small businesses that work out of them every day,” Nantel said.

news.title: Binance Secures $6.5 Billion Freezing Order From Abu Dhabi Court
news.title_en: Binance Secures $6.5 Billion Freezing Order From Abu Dhabi Court

inline_images.caption: Binance SAFU

news.author: Bloomberg
news.article_content:
Binance announced the court action on November 18, saying its legal representatives had identified approximately 26,000 cryptocurrency wallet addresses associated with stolen assets. The exchange plans to maintain an updated list as investigators trace funds moving between wallets and blockchains.

The injunction follows an attack that Binance valued at approximately $6.34 billion. The company previously reported that about $2.85 billion had been frozen or intercepted, leaving substantial assets outside its immediate control.

The ADGM Courts granted a worldwide freezing injunction against unidentified defendants accused of carrying out the theft, alongside separate proprietary injunctions and delivery-up orders intended to support asset recovery.

The $6.5 billion represents the amount covered by the legal order, not the value of cryptocurrency already secured. A freezing injunction restricts dealings with covered assets, while delivery-up orders provide a mechanism for requiring identified assets to be returned.

Some orders involve named parties that previously froze assets linked to the attack. Binance has not alleged wrongdoing by those parties, which include entities cooperating with recovery efforts.

The exchange said certain stablecoin issuers, cryptocurrency exchanges and other intermediaries require judicial authorization before transferring frozen assets to a claimant. The new orders are intended to provide that legal basis where applicable.

Gibson Dunn, the law firm representing Binance, said the orders can be served through blockchain transactions. Its lawyers also described the approximately 26,000 identified wallet addresses as a continuously updated list designed to help intermediaries recognize and restrict stolen funds.

However, identifying an address does not automatically establish that its current balance is recoverable. Effective enforcement depends on the relevant jurisdiction, the assets involved and whether an intermediary can prevent further transfers.

The $6.5 billion figure measures the injunction’s legal scope rather than Binance’s recovered assets. The financial benefit will depend on how much previously frozen cryptocurrency can actually be returned and whether additional stolen funds can be intercepted.

Binance’s earlier incident report placed the total value of affected cryptocurrency at approximately $6.34 billion, with around $2.85 billion frozen or intercepted as of November 3.

The US Department of Justice subsequently announced on November 12 that coordinated government and private-sector efforts had frozen more than $2.7 billion, including more than $1.2 billion covered by US court authorization to seize or restrain assets.

paragraphs: Binance announced the court action on November 18, saying its legal representatives had identified approximately 26,000 cryptocurrency wallet addresses associated with stolen assets. The exchange plans to maintain an updated list as investigators trace funds moving between wallets and blockchains.

The injunction follows an attack that Binance valued at approximately $6.34 billion. The company previously reported that about $2.85 billion had been frozen or intercepted, leaving substantial assets outside its immediate control.

The ADGM Courts granted a worldwide freezing injunction against unidentified defendants accused of carrying out the theft, alongside separate proprietary injunctions and delivery-up orders intended to support asset recovery.

The $6.5 billion represents the amount covered by the legal order, not the value of cryptocurrency already secured. A freezing injunction restricts dealings with covered assets, while delivery-up orders provide a mechanism for requiring identified assets to be returned.
Some orders involve named parties that previously froze assets linked to the attack. Binance has not alleged wrongdoing by those parties, which include entities cooperating with recovery efforts.

The exchange said certain stablecoin issuers, cryptocurrency exchanges and other intermediaries require judicial authorization before transferring frozen assets to a claimant. The new orders are intended to provide that legal basis where applicable.

Gibson Dunn, the law firm representing Binance, said the orders can be served through blockchain transactions. Its lawyers also described the approximately 26,000 identified wallet addresses as a continuously updated list designed to help intermediaries recognize and restrict stolen funds.

However, identifying an address does not automatically establish that its current balance is recoverable. Effective enforcement depends on the relevant jurisdiction, the assets involved and whether an intermediary can prevent further transfers.

The $6.5 billion figure measures the injunction’s legal scope rather than Binance’s recovered assets. The financial benefit will depend on how much previously frozen cryptocurrency can actually be returned and whether additional stolen funds can be intercepted.
Binance’s earlier incident report placed the total value of affected cryptocurrency at approximately $6.34 billion, with around $2.85 billion frozen or intercepted as of November 3.

The US Department of Justice subsequently announced on November 12 that coordinated government and private-sector efforts had frozen more than $2.7 billion, including more than $1.2 billion covered by US court authorization to seize or restrain assets.

Those figures should not be added together. The American enforcement actions concern assets within the broader pool of stolen cryptocurrency, and the announcements do not establish how much of the funds is independently covered by the different legal proceedings.

As FinanceFeeds previously examined, frozen assets are not equivalent to returned funds. Ownership, custody arrangements and judicial procedures can delay recovery even when issuers or exchanges have successfully restricted transfers.

The challenge is particularly pronounced for bitcoin and ether, which lack the centralized issuer controls available for freezing certain stablecoins. Funds held in self-custodied wallets generally cannot be immobilized merely by obtaining a court order.

Separately, Binance announced on November 12 that it had completed coverage of assets affected by the breach, using its corporate treasury, part of its Secure Asset Fund for Users and surplus futures insurance-fund resources.
The exchange also published a new proof-of-reserves snapshot covering 198 tokens. Replenishing customer-facing reserves is nevertheless distinct from recovering the original stolen cryptocurrency.

Successful asset recovery could eventually offset part of the resources Binance deployed to cover the breach. But the exchange does not publish comprehensive audited financial statements, limiting investors’ ability to assess the incident’s ultimate effect on its liquidity, capital and profitability.

The October attack involved unauthorized access to Binance’s internal wallet-signing infrastructure. The exchange’s investigation identified a multistage intrusion involving compromised employee systems, malicious software and unauthorized transaction approvals.
FinanceFeeds previously reported on the compromised development infrastructure and the technical weaknesses that allowed attackers to initiate unauthorized transfers.

The US Justice Department attributed the theft to North Korean military-linked actors known as TraderTraitor. Investigators said the stolen assets were being moved through bridges, mixers and cryptocurrency exchanges, complicating efforts to identify and restrain them.

The evolving wallet-address list could help exchanges and stablecoin issuers identify suspicious deposits before the funds are transferred again. However, tracing cryptocurrency across multiple networks does not establish that investigators retain control over the assets.

Binance’s legal action also comes as the exchange attempts to restore normal operations and continue its international expansion. In a separate development, FinanceFeeds reported that Binance is preparing to enter five additional Asian markets in 2027 while maintaining that it does not need fresh capital following the breach.

For institutional customers, the outstanding considerations extend beyond the size of the injunction. They include the effectiveness of Binance’s revised custody controls, the timing of remaining withdrawal-service restorations and the extent to which the company can recover funds without disrupting its operating reserves.

The ADGM orders strengthen Binance’s legal recovery options but cannot prevent every transfer of stolen cryptocurrency. The most useful indicators of progress will be independently verifiable asset returns, updated recovery balances and evidence that the exchange’s security and liquidity measures remain effective.

celebrity.full_text_en:
$AAPL IS DEVELOPING ITS OWN AI AGENT TO CONTROL DEVICES, BROWSE THE WEB & WRITE CODE

New job listings reveal Apple is building an autonomous AI assistant that can carry out tasks on users' behalf, including:

- Control apps and navigate devices
- Browse the web, run commands and write or debug code
- Plan and execute multistep tasks across apps and services
- Coordinate multiple specialized AI agents

Apple has considered launching the service as early as late 2027, though development is still in its early stages.

Meanwhile, Apple is tightening permissions for competing AI agents on Macs. In macOS 27.3, enabling ChatGPT's computer-use capabilities now requires 14 steps, up from four previously, according to Bloomberg.

celebrity.full_text_en:
Entanglement usually gets top billing in quantum computing, but quantum contextuality, the idea that properties don't have fixed values independent of how you measure them, may be the deeper reason quantum computers can outperform classical ones.

Today on the cover of @ScienceMagazine, we put contextuality to work on our Willow quantum processor:

- won the "impossible" magic square game 98.3% of the time (classical limit: 88.9%)
- measured a 5.59 on state-independent contextuality tests (classical bound: 4, quantum max: 6)
- beat classical strategies in multiplayer games up to 71 qubits
- ran a landmark shallow-circuit algorithm at scale for the first time - up to 105 qubits

These tasks also catch subtle hardware errors random benchmarks miss, a sharper ruler for building better quantum systems. https://t.co/UZOczAeACs
celebrity.full_text_zh:
纠缠通常在量子计算中占据首要位置，但量子上下文性，即属性不具有独立于测量方式的固定值的想法，可能是量子计算机能够超越经典计算机的更深层次原因。

今天，在 @ScienceMagazine 的封面上，我们将上下文应用于我们的 Willow 量子处理器：

- 98.3% 的胜率赢得了“不可能”的魔方游戏（经典限制：88.9%）
- 在与状态无关的上下文测试中测得 5.59（经典界限：4，量子最大值：6）
- 在多达 71 个量子位的多人游戏中击败经典策略
- 首次大规模运行具有里程碑意义的浅电路算法 - 高达 105 个量子位

这些任务还可以捕获随机基准测试遗漏的细微硬件错误，这是构建更好量子系统的更清晰的标尺。

celebrity.full_text_en:
$NVDA & MICROSOFT EXPAND AI PARTNERSHIP FROM AZURE DATA CENTERS TO WINDOWS PCS

Nvidia and Microsoft $MSFT announced several new AI infrastructure and software integrations at Microsoft Ignite, covering cloud computing, enterprise AI models, robotics and local AI.

Here are the key developments:

Vera Rubin on Azure: Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are already running in Microsoft's data centers, with Azure expanding access to Rubin-powered infrastructure for AI training, reasoning and inference.

Enterprise AI models: Microsoft Foundry is expanding support for Nvidia's Nemotron 3.5 open models, allowing companies to customize AI models using their own data and deploy them through Microsoft's cloud services.

55% accuracy improvement, 15x lower cost: EY used Nvidia Nemotron through Microsoft Foundry to improve the accuracy of corporate purchasing-record classification by 55% while reducing costs by 15x compared with proprietary frontier models in its evaluation.

AI on local servers and PCs: Azure Local is adding support for Nvidia RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs and Jetson platforms for industrial AI and robotics. The companies are also demonstrating AI models running directly on Windows PCs powered by RTX Spark.

Microsoft's own AI development: Microsoft AI is using Nvidia Dynamo software to accelerate inference during model post-training, while Nvidia RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs are being used for Bing search models.

The companies are also expanding confidential computing to protect sensitive enterprise models and data during processing on Vera Rubin infrastructure.
celebrity.full_text_zh:
$NVDA 和微软将 AI 合作伙伴关系从 Azure 数据中心扩展到 WINDOWS PC

Nvidia 和 Microsoft $MSFT 在 Microsoft Ignite 上宣布了多项新的 AI 基础设施和软件集成，涵盖云计算、企业 AI 模型、机器人和本地 AI。

以下是主要进展：

Azure 上的 Vera Rubin：Nvidia 的 Vera Rubin NVL72 系统已经在微软的数据中心运行，Azure 扩大了对 Rubin 支持的基础设施的访问，以进行人工智能训练、推理和推理。

企业人工智能模型：微软Foundry正在扩大对Nvidia Nemotron 3.5开放模型的支持，允许企业使用自己的数据定制人工智能模型，并通过微软的云服务进行部署。

准确性提高 55%，成本降低 15 倍：安永在评估中通过 Microsoft Foundry 使用 Nvidia Nemotron，将企业采购记录分类的准确性提高了 55%，同时与专有前沿模型相比，成本降低了 15 倍。

本地服务器和 PC 上的 AI：Azure Local 正在增加对 Nvidia RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU 和 Jetson 平台的支持，以实现工业 AI 和机器人技术。两家公司还展示了直接在由 RTX Spark 提供支持的 Windows PC 上运行的人工智能模型。

微软自己的人工智能开发：微软人工智能正在使用Nvidia Dynamo软件来加速模型后训练期间的推理，而Nvidia RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU则用于Bing搜索模型。

两家公司还在扩展机密计算，以在 Vera Rubin 基础设施处理过程中保护敏感的企业模型和数据。

Standby is a new configuration in the GPT-Live API that lets developers manage periods of inactivity without interrupting the conversation. It's available for both GPT-Live-1 and GPT-Live-1.1.

Set an idle timeout of 5-60 seconds. After that period of silence, the model temporarily pauses, but the WebRTC call stays open at a lower rate ($0.02 per minute vs. the standard $0.05) until someone speaks again.

celebrity.full_text_en:
Cyberattacks are going parabolic, per Bridgewater.

Estimated total cyber incidents have more than doubled since late summer, from about 4,000 a year to nearly 10,000 on a 60-day annualized basis. Over most of the past decade they rose slowly, from about 1,500 in 2017 to roughly 4,000 by mid-2026.

The surge began around the release of the open weights for GLM-5.3, a Chinese AI model from Zhipu AI. Anthropic’s red team had found it could build working cyber exploits. Verified AI-driven cyber incidents have jumped from near zero to more than 200 a year in the same period, including campaigns in which AI agents stole Korean bank and card data.

tools.article_content:
The Justice and Commerce Departments said that they are investigating Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data center company intertwined with the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, after reporting suggested an investigation had been halted last year.

“While we don’t typically comment on ongoing investigations, it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting,” the departments said in a statement issued Monday evening. The departments acknowledged there’s been “significant public attention” on Megaspeed.

Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO last week after reports he had an affair with former Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, who Megaspeed says left the company in August 2025. The scandal has raised questions about national security, and sparked scrutiny of Nvidia’s handling of exports of its chips to China and Megaspeed’s possible role in moving along Nvidia’s chips.

Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that a Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed “came to a sudden halt” late last year after its investigators received an email from Nvidia’s general counsel, claiming Commerce Department official Jeffrey Kessler gave Nvidia permission to reach out. The case was then “quickly” handed over to the DOJ, according to the Times.

> After identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion, the Department of Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations. In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list. Based on the Department of Commerce’s investigation, agents from the Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, conducted an on-site, in-person, end-use check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed CEO Alice Huang. Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.

The statement doesn’t go into detail about the current status of the case, but it says the DOJ and Commerce Department “will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred.”

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 美国司法部与商务部发布声明，确认正就出口管制违规嫌疑对新加坡数据中心企业Megaspeed进行调查。该调查动因涉及前Nvidia CEO黄仁勋辞职引发的公职安全关注，以及该公司在Nvidia芯片流向受限地区过程中的中介角色，目前美方正结合新加坡执法力量进行穿透式审查。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: The U.S. DOJ and Commerce Department have confirmed an investigation into Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed regarding potential export control violations. Triggered by national security scrutiny following the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the investigation probes Megaspeed's intermediary role in the potential diversion of Nvidia chips, with joint enforcement efforts involving Singaporean authorities.

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 此次调查将供应链合规性锚点从芯片分销商前移至数据中心运营商，标志着美方对高性能算力基础设施的“长臂管辖”已进入深水区。对Megaspeed的穿透式审计，将实质性重构东南亚算力基建商的合规风控成本，并可能迫使Nvidia及类似半导体巨头全面重组其海外渠道准入标准。
ai_analysis.insight_en: This investigation shifts compliance scrutiny from chip distributors to data center operators, signaling an expansion of U.S. extraterritorial oversight over high-performance computing infrastructure. The penetration audit of Megaspeed will likely reshape compliance costs for Southeast Asian data infrastructure and force semiconductor giants to restructure their international channel access protocols.

tools.article_content:
Uber Eats customers in a Houston suburb can now have their food delivered by a Zipline drone, the first commercial launch under a partnership announced earlier this year between Uber and the autonomous drone delivery startup.

The commercial partnership kicks off Tuesday in Spring, Texas, before expanding to Dallas. But the companies have far larger ambitions. Uber and Zipline plan to launch drone delivery services in dozens of additional U.S. cities in their collective bid to make one million deliveries per day using the startup’s drones by the end of 2029.

Zipline’s long-range autonomous delivery drones will be used to shuttle food orders weighing up to eight pounds to Uber Eats customers, flying about 300 feet above the ground at speeds of up to 70 miles per hour. Zipline drones don’t land. Instead, the drones lower the orders, which are encased in a small protective pod, to the customer’s location using a tether.

Uber Eats customers in service areas will be able to tap a new “drone” icon on the app’s home page to view all participating restaurants. Uber said that at launch in the Houston area, several nationwide chains, including Jersey Mike’s and Zaxby’s, along with dozens of local restaurants such as Urban Bird and Abu Omar Halal, will offer drone delivery.

“In partnership with Uber Eats we’re going to create a new expectation for delivery in America,” Zipline CEO and co-founder Keller Cliffton said in a statement that underscores those aspirations.

Those nationwide goals mirror the ambitions of other drone delivery companies, including Alphabet-owned Wing and Amazon’s Prime Air service. And those plans have started to collide with concerns from residents in some locations who complain about noise and worry that the drones will disrupt wildlife and pose a risk to safety and privacy.

Companies trying to scale in this nascent industry have argued that delivery via drone is a net benefit for society, citing advantages such as traffic reduction. Customers won’t need to hop in their cars and drive to the store for that forgotten item or takeout order, instead relying on a drone, industry proponents have said.

And while Zipline and other companies have been developing their drones for years, the industry is still in its early days, as is adoption in the communities where services are available.

Zipline, which was founded in 2014, has developed a drone delivery ecosystem that includes aircraft, launch and landing systems, and logistics software. The California-based company’s initial focus was delivering blood in Rwanda, but it eventually expanded its scope to the United States. Its business in the U.S. scaled quickly after receiving its Part 135 air carrier certification from the Federal Aviation Administration in 2022, a critical regulatory hurdle that authorized the company to conduct long-range commercial drone deliveries.

Uber’s partnership extends beyond a commercial relationship with Zipline. The ride-hailing giant also invested in the startup. Neither company has disclosed the investment amount, but Zipline announced last week it had raised $1.5 billion in a round led by Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global, and included backing by Uber, among others.
